gottrg. A SONG OF GOOD COUNSEL. GErtscur AlR—Geniesst den Reitz des Lebens. (TO YOUNG MEN.) Brave boys, would you live wisely, To God and Nature true, Hear me, and I precistly Will tell von what to do. This world's no place for weaving ' Light webs of fancies grand, But for firm will achieving High purpose with strong hand. If weaklings deem it cruel That life so hard should be,l Deem thou all hard things fuel . For victories meant for thee! ' March on, and never weary, With firm aud steady pace; But like the lark be cheery, And skyward turn thy face. Who frets prolongs his sorrow, Who fears makes strong his foe, • And double woe to-morrow I, From golden dreams will flow. Nor dream nor doubt, but stoutly/ The task that nearest lies, Perform, and wait devoutly On God, who helps the wise. He helps no fools, and rightly, Lays vauntful sinners low, Who hold the helm not tightly When windy passions blow. And evermore in danger, With gleesome faith be strong; The devil remains 'a stranger To breasts that teem with song. And never in thy daring Dare for thyself alone, But with thy brother sharing The good that's most thine own. And own the• God who sent thee On life's wide sea to swim, And this glad being lent thee To live and work with Him. —Good Words, July. I. S. .13LyEculE.

WHO ABE THE BRAVE? [The following poem, suggested by the lameitable entes.troplie at Clifton Hall Colliery, is y Mr. Ben Brierley. It has been vrinted for sale, aud the proceeds will be given to Zia relief fund... 3 Who are the biave? These who in battles strde,' Heedless of danger, charge the -unknown foe, And hand to hand contendiag—life to Ife The stake—the vict'ry wen by fatal blow? Not mine the task to sere the: warrior's wretth' Though red his sword, and blunted in its.aheath But they are braver who at duty's call, Far in the reaches of the treacherous mine,'" Face dangers that would pant lieartsappal, To save, not slay—mercy with love combine— Firm at their post—no care themselves to save— The.choice "twint safety and a threatened grave— Choose to brave death with blaikestrterrors drest, Rather than one should perita by their flight! And though the tibias of-cloom might strike :the breast, And sweep them to regions tf eternal night, Heed not repeated cads from Aeberonis gate— "(in, aave yourselves„ and leave us to our fate."* And tlais'mongst shrieks, andlrayers, and dying groans, And jabbericgdai_ocy,t more dreadful still 'Than cries for kelp, ,or breath-exhausting moans— Tire terror-stricken Smits with horrors.fill; And showers of wreck mist down upon the way To blessed hope, the .assuring eye of day. Bow shall we sing their praise, the noble band, Who not in knightly .jonst,..er warlike fray, Bush on each ether at a king's.comniand, But they who Mercy's call at once obey, Short farewells breathe, then plunge in:gloom pro- found Uncertain of return to safer ground? At such brave deeds si nation's heart upheaves, And pours its blessings "with substantial aid; And bastes to chronicle on virgin leaves Tributes of praise to none batheroes paid; And the Grist God, in mercy looking down, Sees in these mea the fittest. for his crown.

It is all very well to have a dock en the stairs, but it is not at all desirable to have it run dawn and strike one. - "What is the matter with the baby?" asked a lady of a little girl, whose baby brother she understood to be ailing. "Oh, nothin' much," was the answer. "He's onlyhatchin' teeth." During an examination of a witness as to the locality of the stairs in the house, the counsel asked him "Which way do the stairs run?" The witness, a noted wag, re- plied, "One way they run upstairs, and the other way they run downstairs." The learned counsel winked his eyes, and then took a look at the csiling. The lady of the house was a handsome woman of a , mature order of be laity, and when she had finished her toilet she gazed fondly at herself in the glass, and re- marked to her new maid, "You'd give 'a good deal to be as good looking as I am, wouldn't you now ?" "Yesi'm ; almost as much as you would give to be as young as I am." It is not believed this epigrammatic young woman l will be chosen again at the expiration of her present term. A JAPANESE FABLE.—Once upon a time there was in Japan a stonecutter, a simple workman in the quarries. His life was rude, he worked much, gained little, and was not at all satisfied with his fate. "Oh, if I could only be rich enough to rest, to sleep on thick matting, wrapped in a kiriman of soft silk I" Such was the sigh he breathed to heaven. An angel heard it. "It shall be according to thy desire," said the angel to him. And he at once became rich, and his rested: slept upon thick matting, and wrapped himself in a kiriman of soft silk. It happened that the Emperor passed by. He was pre- ceded by heralds on horseback, followed by a 'brilliant escort of cavaliers, and surrounded by persons who held over his head an immense parasol, resplendent with gold. "What good does it do to me to be rich," murmured the man, "as long as I have not the right to go out with an escort, and my head protected by a parasol? Why ain. I not an Emperor?" "Thou shalt be," said the angel. And indeed he became the Emperor. He had an escort before and behind him, and people who held above him an inimenge parasol resplendent with gold. However, the sun, with its arden beams, dried up the country, and the dusty roads, quivering with its brightness, fatigued ' the eyes. "What's the advantage to be an Emperor ?" cried the man, "when the heat of the day exhausts you, and the sun never ceases to make you feel his power? But if one could be the sun!" " Behold ! are you satisfied ?" the angel asked, for he had become the sun, and he darted his beams up and down, right and left, and, all around him, and he scorched the herbage of the earth and the faces of the princes of the earth. But now a cloud thrust itself between the earth and him. It held back the rays of the sun, and prevented them from falling upon the earth's surface. "There is strength," cried the man, "d 7 cloud capable of resisting my power; it Would be better if I were a cloud." "Very well, replied the angel. And the t ransi formation was at once accomplished. The new cloud Paced itself haughtily between the sun and the earth, and so thoroughly intercepted the rays of the sun that it s(sul saw the earth covered with its shadow. Then it caused the big drops of rain, and pourng .showers, and waterspouts to fall on the land, so that the torrents burst their bounds, and the rivers spread over and devasted the fields. Nothing resisted the force of the inundation; only a rock defied it, perfectly motion- less. In vain the bellowing waters beat upon it in their fury.; the rock yielded not, but the foaming waves died at its feet. "A rock, then. is my superior," said the cloud; "I would rather bi's in its place." "You shall be," said the angel. And he was formed into a steep, unshaken rock, insensible to the rays of the sun, indif- ferent to the torrents of the rain and the shock of the tumultuous waves. But he distinguished at his foot a mail Of poor appearance, hardly clothed, armed with a chisel and a hammer, and the man, with the help of those instruments,struck pieces off the rock, which he dressed into stone proper for cutting. "What is that ?" cried the rock; "has a man the power of rending pieces of stone from my base? Shall Ibe weaker than he ? Then it is absolutely necessary that I should be that man." "Have your wish,' said the angel. And he became again what he had been—a poor stone-cutter, a simple workman in the quarries. flip life was rude; he worked hard and gained little; but he had learnt contentment with his lot. A farmer purchased some supplies, among Which was a pint of whisky. To avoiit breakage he placed the bottle in a box 'of rice, but outreaching torohe found that, the bottle was broken and the rice saturated. Hethrowthe rice behind the barn, anal a big turkey paid his respects to it. In dm time the turkey became dead drunk, and was found in that condition by the farmer, who thought that disease or poison had killed him. The bird was still warm, and the death evidehtly recent. The farmer would not eat him himself, but plucked him for market, and left him in the stabie. The next morning be found the bereft gobbler shivering naked on his roestaand look- ing at him with reproachful eyes. ' A Tamar TAKING A Shinaow.—The following' incident, showing the voracity of a brown trout, was related to an Irish correnpondent of, the Field a few days age by an English genaleMan who had been -fishing ahWaterville. While trout fishing one day in the little river which con- nects Lough Curran° or Waterville Lake with the sea, his man hooked, just above the bridge which spans the near end of the river, a fish which gave him a consider- able amount of play. He succeeded in landing it, Mr. Hotchkinsciming up in the meantime. The Tzah proved to be a brown trout weighiag lalb., and appeared un- usually plump and fat. 'Mr. Hdtchkins, observing the dis- tended appearance of the stomach, ordered leis man' to rip it open, when to his astonishment he found a fully- fledged sparrow, quite perfect, withoat even a feather disturbed, and which he said could not have been many ninnies in the trout's stomach. His curiosity still fur- ther aroused by this strange discovery, he -searched the arch of the bridge, and there found a sparrow's nest with 'several yonagobirds in it. "HE'LL NEVER SET THE THAMES Ott ,FTRE."—Many years ago, before' machinery was introduced into flour mills for the purpose of sifting the flour, at was the cus- tom of the,miller to send it home unsifted. The process of sifting was done thus, but principaLlyin Yorkshire The " temse," or sieve, wlalch was provided with a rini which projected from thebottom of it, was worked over the mouth of the barrel into which the flees or meal was sifted. An active fellow, who worked bard, not unfre- quently set the rim of the" temse" on fire by force of friction against the rim of the flour barrel; so that, in fact, this -part of domestic ecnployment became a stan- dard by which to test a man's will or capacity to work hard; and thus of a lazy , fellow, or one deficient in strength, it was said, "He will never set the temse on fire." The long mis-use of the word. tense for sieve, as well as the superseding of hand labour by machinery in this. particular species of work, may possibly have tended to the substitution of sound for sense, in such phrases as a He will never set the Thames on fire," the Mersey on fire, or any other river—Oxos. DOES MACHINERY SPARE LABOUR ?—We deplore the loss of time and waste of labour of the poor Otaheitan or Marquesan alothirtaker working at his rough mats, when we see power looms running off easily and exactly miles of finely-finished and comfortable fabrics ; we pity the dusky Hindoo printer, who has as much diffi- culty in executing one spot of his rude pattern as our cylinders overcome in covering fifty yards of calico with an intricate, many-coloured, and beautiful design. But much of this acquisition of power has beedused only to increase production. The 'deckhand On hoard the British steam vessel. the - stoker in her hold, work harder .far than the boatmap on the Nile; the Kaffir or Hottentot .. wagon driver eijoys a life of calm repose compared with ' the engine -driver or his assistants; the smith calmly, tempering the Toledo blade woald look with ,amazement on the activity and energy of the attendants of the steam hammer ; the South Sea Islander is used to no such long hours as the women and children of our cotton factories; and the listless Hindoo would almost as soon he blown from a canon's mouth at once as spend his life in the active, intelligent operations of machine printing.—Labour, Leisure, and Luxury, 4,y Alexander Wylie. SAVER) EY DICK Tommta—aly mother's cousin, Cathe- rine, wife of a purser in the navy, and conspicuous for her beauty and impulsive, violent temper, having quar- relled with her excellent sister, Dorothea Fryer, at whose house in Staffordshire she was staying, suddenly set off ' to London on a visit to her great-uncle, the Rev. John Plimley, Prebend of the Collegiate Church at Wolver- hampton and Chaplain of Morden College, Blackheath. ' She journeyed by the ordinary mode of conveyance, the Gee-Ho, a large stage-waggon drawn by a team of six horses, and which, driven merely by day, took a week from Wolverhampton to the Cock and Bell, Smitkfield. Arrived in London, Catherine proceeded on foot to Black- heath; there, night having come on and losing her way, she was suddenly accosted by a horseman with, "Now, 'my pretty girl, where are you going?" Pleased by his gallant address, she begged him to direct her to Morden -Colle. He assured her that she was fortunate in having met with him, instead of one of his company, and in- ; ducing her to mount before him, rode across the heath I to the pile of buildings which had been erected bya Sir Christopher Wren for decayed merchants, the recipients of Sir John Morden's bounty. Assisting her to alight, he rang the bell, then remounted his steed and galloped away, 'but not before the alarmed official who had answered the summons had exclaimed, " Heavens ! Dick Turpin on Black Bess !"—" Reminiscences of Illy Life," by Mary gowitt, in "Good Words." How TO LIFT THE BtRDEN.—" My son," said a sa- gacious parent, "put that load on the waggon." "I cannot, father," replied the boy. "It weighs many tons, and exceeds the strength of a hundred men." "You can put it on the waggori, and I will teach you how. Chop-and split it into lengths suitable to your strength. Now let this be a lesson to you. All through life you will find heavy burdens to carry, heavy tasks to per- form. Do not Inspect them in bulk and become dis- heartened, neither grapple nor attempt to master them with one effort. Perform what your strength will per- mit—a little each hour—each day. You will gradually become strong, and meet with success in the end. By attempting to lift a heavy log at one effort you might injure yourself beyond recovery. But by lifting a little at a that() you would in a lifetime move more logs than could be stored in a township. Great success in life is secured by knowing your strength and lifting accord- ingly; by continuous and persistent effort rather than a monetary struggle. There,is another way in which you can move heavy, logs. There are many inventions de- signed for this purpose, the existence of which you do not suspect. In some instances you are only required to attach the grappling hooks and the burden is borne wherever you desire. Remember that in all undertak- ings in life there is one way to proceed much better than all others. Investigate closely, assuring yourselves that you are working by the best methods. Otherwise you will be lifting the log without appliance. Only the best methods lead to success in this progressive and competitive age. If you cannot discover these methods you will find your rivals pushing ahead. You will be outrun in the race." - BISMARCK'S WORK AND METHOD.—Frorn the beginning of his career his one thought, his "sole guiding star," as he calls it, himself, has been how to make, first Prussia and now Germany, "breathe freely in the world as a great nation." Now the aggrandisement of Prussia—the creation of a strong, industrial, Protestant, progressive Power in Central Europe has certainly been a benefit, not only to that country itself, but to the general cause of order and civilisation. But whatever may be thought of the work itself, when judged by its results, there can be nothing but unsparing condemnation for the absolute .disregard, not only of human life, but of the greater con- siderations of truth and justice, by means ea which it was effected. Of all modern statesmen, Bismarck is the most openly and cynically Machiavellian. He lives for the greater good of the Prussian State, as the Jesuit does for the greater good of the Church. That is the one thing in life that is an end, all other things are only means and of means he asks no question but whether they are effec- tive; if they are effective they are good; if they are ineffective, nothing can justify them. Principles, alli- ances, human lives, partrties, things of any sort which other Men may count sacred, are all, according to the habit of Bismarck's mind, regarded in the light of mere political -instrumentalities that exist to be utilised, and may with perfect indifference be fostered to-day and sacrificed to-morrow, just as Imperial interests may seem to dictate. Under these circumstances, his career natu- rally exhibits many inconsistencies, -but consistency in his opinion is not a merit in politics. As he told Jules Fevre, at Versailles, it often leads to pernicious obsti- nacy. "I have been taught by experience," he said, "and I never hesitate to sacrifice personal feeling to the requirements of the hour. Our country must be served and not dominated."—Good Words. • 1

SEEOI.SIfTIV6 AND WEST MIDLAND AGRICDLTDRAL SOCIETY.—Thm entries for this society's show, which takes place e.t Knighton on July 22nd, 23rd, and 24th, are as follows :—Horses 112, cattle 121, sheep 153, pigs 26, cheese and butter 38, wool 11, total 461. It will thus be seen that the exhibition this year will be of a very important character. Sir-John Lawes has during the past season conducted same experiments upon the relative values of ensilage .and roots, and it would appear that the results he has published have up to the present not given complete satisfaction to the supporters of the ensilage system. A correspondent states that Mr. Thomas Tickner, of Stockbridge Farm, Romney Marsh, a well-known breeder of Kent sheep, has recently shorn his rams, and has ob- . tained the following weights per fleece :-1 three-year- ; old ram, 201bs. ; 1 two-year-old ram, /81bs,; 3 two-year- -1 olilaras, each 171bs. _. ___. . . .

---, - VALUATIONS OF SHEEP STOCK.—The Whitsunday stock valuations of 1885 in the North are all but over, and considering the low prices store sheep have been inking in the public market., it is surprishig to And valuators putting such high prices upon them when taken over by 4ucoming tenants. Seeing the risk ifigoing tenants have cf being overcharged for stock taken over by valuation, this system is now a great drawback on entering stock farms; and considering the many facilities that now exist for acquiring and selecting stock in the open market, it is strange hew farmers still submit to take over stock on this footing; and as to the valuators, we wonder that they allow themselves to he the instigators of such a difference in the price of stock taken over at their valuation, and the actual value, er 'what the lame stock would realise in the open market. THE WARBLE FLY.—Since hearing of the illness of cattle supposed to have been caused by applying mer- curial ointment to kill warble maggots, Miss E. A. Orme- rod has added a caution to her pamphlet on warble ily. In the pamphlet stockowners are advised to destroy the warble maggot, when it has so far matured that the black end of the tail is visible, by "just touching it with a little mercurial ointment." To this advice the following note 'is appended :—" Should not on any ac- count be used as a smear. Mc.Bougal's dip, lard with a little carbolic acid, or tar alone, had better be tried when there is fear of careless application." Miss Ormerod has been investigating: the case of the affected cattle, which became ill a fortnight after the application of mercurial ointment. INTERESTING PRIVATE DAIRYING EXPERI3IPINTS.—ME.
Long writes :—‘" Thereis a distinct advance in: private

dairy-ing. Oneof the best new ventures I know—is that of Mr. John Swami, of Lincoln' who is -celebrated for the quality of his ensilage, which took the -champion prize at the ensilage show in London. This gentleman determined that in starting his dairy upon a modern system he would do nothing by halves, and bearing in mind the fact that town consumers of milk, prefer the best they can get, especially when they pay a good price, he obtained & number of Jersey ,vows, the majority of which were specially selected by himself in the island,' and which now reach a total of 45 bead in all. There is much in Mr. Swami's system of management which it is well to know. The milk, which is unusually rich, when kept for butter-making is passed through the Danish centrifugal separator; which skims seven gallons of cream per hour. This cream is left to ripen for4B hours 'before it is churned, and, as •I have frequently recom- mended, it is salted in the churn with brine instead of with salt in its solid state. The advantage of this is that the butter can be much more regularly salted, the brine being added when it is in its granular state, so that every small particle Of butter comes into contact with the brine. When the lattevis,rim off, if the butter is too salt, it can be made milder by one or two washings of cold water. Another idea which I should like to follow with close interest is that the calvesare fed from a week old upon linseed jelly and skim milk. The milk is not hailed, bsrtbaked to a steaming ;temperature, and given with the linseed at 90 deg., the calves 'taking it from a patent feeder, one Of Which is given to every pair. Again, strange to say, Mr. Swann's cows are not turned out at all upon the pasture, but are fed ainder cover the , whole of the year through, their chief food being ensi- lage, of which they get 361 b. per day, with a bran mash and a little pollard, cottoncake,' or oats, Iron troughs are used for water, rock salt is kept in each, and the bedding is of German peat moss. Thus Mr. Swann has introduced several modern features, allot which deserve study. If, as may be presumed, his success with ensi- lage as a food for cows is ,continued—and we may as- sume that it is as he is building more silos—it is another proof that ensilage is ,one of the most valuable new features inlfeonnection with dairy stock:" CARE or SWINE.—None of our farm animals answer more quickly to, or yield more profit from, good treat- ment than swine; and in many localities none are more neglected than these homely, but useful, animals. In the west where hogs run at large and follow the droves of feeding steers, their management after they are wsaned is very simple, but where hogs are keptin yards or pens and are expected to subsist mainly on skimmed milk, or the refuse from the kitchen, more care is neces- sary, and their wants must be carefully attended to, or. they will not thrive as they ought. The most important thing to remember in feeding hogs is, that there is no such thing as "stock order;" the pig...that is not so fed that it gains in weight continually and rapidly is not a profitable animal, and soon eats more feed than it is worth. Many farmers keep a pen of store hogs in low condition through the winter, a a dead less; the pigs do not grow, and yet eat almost as much as the fatten- ing hogs. Here, again, ;we come to the "food of sup- port." The larger part of the pig's food is needed to keep him alive, and prevent him from going backward; and a very little more food, ludiciously applied, will usually make all the difference between prodt and loss in keeping pigs. The cheapest pork is that made from pigs which have been fed on all that they would eat. If it does not pay to make pork by liberal feeding, it does not pay to make it at all, and it had better be given up. The care of pigs should begin as soon as they are born; sometimes the sows are very savage, and, if not pre- vented, will eat the pigs as soon as they appear. If a sow shows this disposition she should 150 watched and the pigs taken from her. When her labour is finished, they should be carefully put down, beside her, and she Will generally take up with them at once. The pen for breeding sows shouldlie roomy and warm, and the floor ' nearly level, so that the weight of her body will not settle down and crush the pigs.

REARING CALVES. Dr. Aitken, chemist to the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, in a lecture on the above subject, pointed out that the kind of food which. contained the greatest proportion of protein or albumenoid substance was the most nourishing for building up the bodies of animals. By the aid of a large chart he showed the various constituents of different kinds of food. Some kinds of hay had double the amount of protein that others had. Clover was a more nutritious hay than any , other, and wheat straw was not so nourishing as oat straw. Crushed beans were very high in nourishing , power. Linseed cake stood very high, and rape cake higher still. In inferior hay there was less protein, and, of course, less feeding power. Meadow grass contained considerable protein, and Clover was very high in,its digestibility, having a great deal of protein. Vetches also ranked very high as a nourishing food. The fourth of the whole part of beans given an animal was diges- tible, and nearly a, third of the whole of linseed cake was digestible, and the same as regards rape cake. In certain periods of an animal's growth there was a ratio of protein which was best suited for the particular stage of its fattening. It was not the quantity of food given to an animal which they had to look to so much, as its nourishing quality. They might give an ox as much as they liked, say, of wheat straw, and if it was in a poor condition, it might be able to keep it living; and if given to an animal in a fairly good condition it would not tend to make it, much the better. Therefore, it was neces- sary, in feeding an animal on wheat straw, to add a little linseed cake to make up for the poverty of its nourishing power., So that the nutrient ratio of feed- ing stuffs was of great importance. Good hay was very nutrient, but there was a hay which required something containing more protein than it afforded itself. Dr. Aitken then showed, by the help of another large chart, the maintenance ratio and the fattening ratio of the different elements of food, and went on to say that sheep -were able to take a more nitrogenous or nburishing diet than cattle. Wrightson's book on "Agriculture" would give them.proper directions for their guidance in the fat- tening of animals. He showed from a table the composition of the food which a calf required from its earlier to its later stages. It always got less and less albutnenoid matter, and more of the starchy kind of food. In the process of fattening an ox, its food should gradually be diminished as it nears its prime condition, for its stomach was not then so capacious as formerly when in a lean condition. He then referred to an illustration of the intestines of an animal, showing the processes of di- gestion, which he described in a very interesting man- ner. He alluded to what lie had said in his first lecture as to the birth of the calf and the necessity of its getting the colustrum,.or the milk of. the mother, which at that

time was so highly albumenoid in its chawter. Starchy food was afterwards required to prevent the nitrogenous or albumenoid food from being unnecessarily used up. In nourishing calves, great care should be taken to keep their food as near in its quality to the nourishment they obtained before birth.—Milk: A calf should not be taken off its mother's milk before ten days; and if after that, they should make its milk half skim milk, then as its proper nourishment will be so much lowered, the fist squeezed out of linseed cake will be found useful in en- riching its diet. Oatmeal porridge or barley meal por- ridge does very well after the calf is a few 'weeks old.

div.p: ttilq; THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 4, 1885. '.,1 COTTAGE GARDENING I "AS I WENT SAILING."

'Though the much needed rain fell on the I.9tikit did not have the effect oneivould have expected till the 23rd, and vegetation, instead of being excited and stimulated, receistct a slight shock from the roughness and coldness of the north-westerly wind as well as from a pelting hailstorm on the morning of the 21st. The latter, however, may have been only local. Since the rain we have been able to thin the spring sown Onions, which were so firm in the soil that it was not possible previously to draw them out in the ordinary way. Some people make a mistake over their Onion bed byliouncing ,en the largest as soon as there are any fit to pull, and they follow this rule till the bed is satisfactorily thinned, by which it is obvious that the most puny plants will have been left. Either there should be a small plot set apartand sown thickly for the purpose of laving young Onions to draw, or patience must be exercised until there are plenty of large ones in the bed. Our plan is to babve the smallest, and continue selecting in that way till we have each Onion four inches distant. If there are gaps to any extent those pulled up will do well trans- .planted, especially when such weather as we are now •experiencing prevails. Care should be taken not to put the bulb in deeper than it has been, as well as to press the soil firmly round the roots, which must . be directed perfectly straight down. Beetroot should be also fit for thinning, and the surplus plants will do to fill gaps, which are.frequently numerous from the action of slugs. The roots of these also must be put down straight, but the soil need net be pressed so firmly around them es for Onions. If the beetroot rows are 10in, distant tile plants should'be Bin. apart in the row. Parsnips unfor- tunately have not succeeded with us •hitherto when transplanted, so we have given up the attempt. We have since the change in the weather been :busily en- gaged in planting out of the seed beds. The following autumn and winter vegetable—Coleworts a kind of small Cabbage found to come in very useful some sea- sons. "'St. John's Day Cabbage we have also planted, and for autumn or late suminer use there is nothing we , know of in the Cabbage line to equal it. Savoys follow : these, and they may all,' be planted % distance of lft. each wig unless the large variety of Savoys is grown. The other subjects have been the various sorts of Bale , and Broccoli. Where ground is not ready to receive them they should be pricked out3in. distant, rather than allow them to remain thick in the seed bed to injure L each other. This plan should be practised in all gardens that are infested with slugs, so as to secure strong, woody stems, that will offer greater resistance to the -slug's bite. THE FRONT GARDEN.—This is a good time to divide Polyanthus and Primroses, if it is necessary to increase the stock, or if any are taio large or have been standing the same,ground for any length of time. We find they flower more freely the first year or two after being divided, which is no doubt cite to the fresh soil round their roots. We fear the wind and rain came upon some of us a little too soon, and many things were found blown on their sides, which would not have occurred had they been staked. To secure them from further in- jury, all plants that carry heads of flowers and stand more than a foot high will need supports, and those that form bushes more than that in diameter ought to have three or four stakes round, on which a string should be twisted, so that it may not slip down but form a secure b ind round the whole. Large Lupin bushes require five such stakes; and frequently two bands. The rule-should be, in tying all plants, to avoid that besom- like method which we frequently see, and allow the plant to preserve its natural position. THE WINDOW.—Most a the plants that usually oc- cupy the window.are now best outside on warm days, and more especially in showery weather. lit must, how- ever, be borne in mind that the plants must be made secure against any possibility of the wind blowing them over, or in a few minutes after they are put out the un- lucky owner may find all on their sides, and the pots, if not the plants, smashed. We have seen them placed outside the window, and a string stretched in front of them and attached to two nails on either side of the window frame. This affords but little security unless each plant is tied to the string, .and it is obvious if the plants fall laterally they must inevitably roll underneath the string. The better plan viould be to nail a board in front of the pate.

RT THOMAS GIBBONS. Author of "Boxing the Compass," " Naval Songs and Song Writers," " The Way to Ichang," dm. No. IL—ON THE THRESHOLD OF COREA. My dream* crowd thick and fast, when wintry gales sweep o'er the coast with sharp and Icy tneatn, Chanting anon in loud and fitful waits, Their never ending song of wre?k and death. But this, the wildest and the most impressing, Came in the sweet, calm days a summer time, When Nature smiLd, the Corean valleys dressing In all the glories of.a tropic clime. Gamma R. WILLIS. In. 1871 it was planned that an expedition, consisting of the ships forming the American fleet in Asiatic waters should -visit Cores. The Hon_ F. F: Low, the United States Minister in China, was charged with the task of negotiating a treaty with the Government of Corea. As is shown by a paragraph in the instructions emanating from the Secretary of State to Minister Low, no hostile measures were contemplated. "The department relies upon you," runs the document, "to exercise prudence and discretion, to maintain firmly the right of the United States to have their seamen protected, to avoid a conflict by force unless it cannot be avoided without dishonour, and to seek in all proper ways the harmonious and ' friendly assistance of the Chinese Government." Though Cores is situated on a peninsula within a few hours' steam of the open Northern ports of China, and for centuries has maintained some sort, of intercourse with that empire and Japan, the country, in all its rela- ,tions, is 'almost unknown to the nations of the West. The several expeditions visiting the coast, while ascer- taining the fact that spacious harbours, navigable rivers, and luxuriant vegetation abound, failed to penetrate the seclusion beyond. Several adventurous spirits among the Jesuits have traversed the borderland, and lingered with the strange people, but those hardy religionists have left the seal of mystery unbroken. The English, the French, and in 1868 the United States ship Shenan- doah, have sailed along the beautiful margin of the little-known land. The English contented themselves with surveying, but the French under A dmiral Raze, having a desire to visit the Corean capital, were driven to their ships; while the American commander Febiger, after kindly entertaining some of the natives on board the Shenandoah, went his peaceful way. From time to time, adventurous nomads, lured by strange tales of fabulous wealth, hoping, Jason-like, to bear away the Golden Fleece, have attempted to pass inland, but death has'met most of them on the very threshold. In 1865, a steamer, called the General Sherman, flying the American flag, voyaged thither from Shanghai, but no word of her crew ever came to those anxiously awaiting tidings in the outer world. The General Sher- man was commanded by a Captain Preston, and manned by Manilamen and Chinese. Outside Some general mer- . chandise her cargo consisted of rifles, pistols, and war 'material. Ostensibly she went to Corea for the purposes of trade, but whisperers have assigned other objects held in view by the adventurers. The vessel reached the Salee river. At the time it was currently reported that. the natives were willing to barter with the strangers, but the Corean officials objected, and requested the vessel's departure. Preston, whatever else was his object, had -no intention of leaving; and forced his passage up the river, deeming his crew of Manilamen capable of resist- ing any attack promoted by the officials. The sequel proved otherwise; the Coreans boarded the vessel, driving the crew below, fastened the hatches down, and set fire to the ship! That was the story carried to Shanghai by some Chinese junk sailors. It would seem, then, the Coreans had some foundation for declaring that the vessel was . blown up, during an engagement "brought on by overt ads of hostility from her own crew," and that all on board perished by the explosion; notwithstanding, others will insist to the contrary.' However', while this in- humanity is charged againtst them, it is worth remem- bering that an American schooner, the Surprise, was wrecked on the Corean shores in 1864, and that the ' sailors were rescued, kindly treated, and escorted safely 1 to China. I The United States Squadron rendezvoused at Nagasaki, Japan, May, 1871, where preparations were made for the . expedition. It comprised the Colorado, bearing the flag L of Rear Admiral John Rodgers, the Alaska, Benicia, Monocacy, and Palos ; the whole force mounted 15 guns, and numbered 1,230 officers and men. On the 16th of May, a bright and pleasant morning, the fleet weighed anchor, and leaving the beautiful bay of Nagasaki be- hind, stood atit to sea. The west coast of Corea—high, rugged, and picturesque—was sighted on the morning of the 19th, and the same afternoon the fleet came to anchor off Boisee Island, near the mouth of the Salee River. Owing to the water shoaling beyond this ancho- rage, it was decided to make the headquarters of the expedition at Beige Island., where, with the other islands, it forms a bay into which the river flows. The Coreans were not long in learning of the presence of strangers on their coast. Very soon after the fleet anchored, a junk flying a white flag was espied steejing towards the ship, and it was quickly, alongside the Colorada. A party of Corean officers, styling themselves ambassadors, bearing a letter, stepped on board the fri- gate. It was very evident they were not officials from the Capital., The Commander-in-Chief, while declining to , see them; directed the interpreters to say the Minister • and himself would only hold conference with officers of State, properly accredited from the King. Still, he de- sired them to Inform the people of the peaceful inten- tions of the American forces; that be wished to reach the capital, and establish friendly relations with the Government. He would survey the river in the direction of Seoul, but, in order to enable them to bear the mes- sage and assure the natives, the survey would be delayed a few days. The dusky visitors departed, but it is well to transcribe the letter they left behind them. Translated, it read somewhat as follows ; "A man of your nation, whose name was Febiger, came here and communicated and then went away. Why' cannot you do the same? A people called the French came here, and we refer you to them for what happened. This people and kingdom have lived in the enjoyment of their civilisatidn four thousand years, and we want no other. We trouble no other nations. Why should they tiouble us? 'Our country is in the extreme East, ancj - yours in the extreme West. For what purpose do you come so many miles across the sea? Is it to inquire about the vessel destroyed? Her men committed piracy and murder, and they were punished with death. Do you want our land? That cannot be. Do you want inter- course with us? That may never be." Wrapped in a civilisation and freedom peculiar and en- joyable to themselves, with an unbending. aversion to foreigners, one can understand the many interrogation points the Corean wri,ter crowded into this caustic mis- sive. Dr. Williams, glancing at the trade between China and Corea,•quoting Annalis de la Propagation, remarks:— " There are many restrictions upon this intercourse by both Governments, which forbids their subjects passing and re-passing the frontiers. The trade is conducted at fairs, under the supervision of officers and soldiers, and the short time allowed for concluding the bargains, and the great numbers resorting to them, tender them more like the frays of opposing clans than the scenes of peace- able trade. There is a market town in Cores itself, called Ki-iu-wan, about four leagues from the frontier, where the Chinese supply the Careens with dogs, cats, pipes/ leather, stags' horns, copper, horses, mules, and asses ; and receive in exchange baskets, kitchen utensils, ricie, corn, swine, paper, mats, oxen, furs, and small horses. Only four, or five hours are allowed to conduct this fair, and the Cdrean officers, under whose charge it is placed, drive all the strangers back to the frontier as soon as the day closes." On the Ist of June, Commander Homer C. Blake, of the Alaska, was ordered to proceed with the survey. Approaching noon, on the flood tide, the Monaco,cy and the Palos got under weigh, steering in for the river, four steam launches going ahead to obtain soundings. Near , the enVance of the river, on a sharp point branching into the stream, a Art of formidable appearance, rendered by nature doubly effective as ' a place of defence, was espied crowning the position, while on the steep acclivi- ties commanding the river, and on the low-lying shores, a line of watch-towers and batteries was visible. A , large yellow banner, inscribed with Chinese characters, floated over the fort, while hundreds of van-coloured flags waved from the batteries on the hill-sides. Close to its mouth the river narrows, and round the fortified point the current swept with great strength, necessitating a sharp outlook to keep the boats manageable. The point was almost reached, the steam launches were quite abreast of it, and about heading for still water near the shore, when the report of a signal gun was heard, and instantly the American seamen in the open launches were fired upon from the low-lying batteries. The im- - perfect aim of the Coreans saved the sailors. The seamen quickly returned the fire, manning the howitzers in the bows of the boats; and very soon the Ditonocacy and Palos joined in the chorus, The rapid and accurate firing of the Americans quickly silenced the lower batteries and the Coreans took to the hills. About half- past three firing ceased, and the gunboats, having4the launches in tow, turned down the stream, reaching the anchorage off Bois& Island at six o'clock. The Corean Government failed to mak4in apology for the attack on the surveying party. At various times Ithe Corean officers appeared on the beach bearing letters to the Commander-in-Chief, demanding that thg strangers would leave the coast. After a time it was decided to land a force from the ships and punish the Coreans for firing on the United States flag; Kang-hao Island, where the citadel was visible, being the selected fighting ground. On the morning of the 10th of June, the Monocacy arid Palos, having 19 boats in tow, and four steam launches in company, started for the river. Passing two forts, both of which were silent, the Monocacy opened with a broad-side on the third one, and the fire was briskly returned by the enemy. But the Coreans again retreated to the hills. It was now expedient to land the men from the boats, and this was safely effected, notwithstanding the rapid current and dangerous navigation. The landing foree, consisting of officers., sailors, and marines, formed ten companies of infantry and manned seven pieces of field artillery; in all numbering six huhdred and fifty men. The Coreans had fled, entrenching themselves in great numbers on the opposite heights. The sailors took possession of the lower fort, and the artillery was advanced to command the position-held by the natives. As yet, there was no fighting at close quarters; the Coreans contented themselves with keeping up an un- certain fire as they retreated, evidently manceuvring to draw their enemy into a trap. But the day was waning;

the difficult tramp, through mud and marsh and over wild hill sides, under a fierce sun, and the immense toil required to advance the guns, had tended to harass and fatigue the men, and the position being a favourable one, the force encamped for the night. On the 11th of June the reveille sounded at day-break, and the invading force pushed forward. .Meanwhile, the Coreans gathered into the citadel, greeting the sailors , with loud shouts. and keeping up a steaily fire from jingals and .matchlocks. Under cover of the ships' guns the sailors advanced and stormed the stronghold. Now was the time that really told the character of the foe! The outlying batteries were desperately defended; but steadily advancing up the steep glacis, firing as they went, the blue-jackets soon worked their way to close quarters. A lieutenant and two others, a sailor and marine, fell mortally wounded. The corn-age of the de- fenders was sublime, seeking death rather than retreat,; but their long spears and matchlocks were almost useless against revolver and cutlass; and their daring bravery and stubborn resistance forced the work of slaughter. On the west side of the citadel the fighting was fttrious; the Coreans, unable -to reload their guns rolled huge rocks and hurled large stones on their assailants. When compelled to give way, though rallying several times, many attempted to fight through the reserves, but were almost instantly cut down or captured; while others, re- trefning to the batteries in the valley and on the point, exposed themselves to a murderous fire from the squad of artillery posted on the adjacen thill top ; others plunged into the river, or east themselves headlong over the rugged cliffs; and of the intrepid garrison only about twenty prisoners were taken, many of them being badly wounded. How desperately those pagan warriors de- fended their seclnded homesteads! Chanting their war dirge, a blood-chilling cadence which nothing can dupli- cate, to the last handful of men they persistently fought themselves into eternity, seeking no quarter, and dis- playing a courage which was really grand. Nearly two hundred and fifty of their dead were counted in and around the works of the citadel they had so nobly de- fended; while others perished in the river, or were shot in the ravines. The American force lost three killed, and eight were wounded. Forty-seven battleflags were • captured, and the standard of the Corean commander fell into the hands of the invaders. In the afternoon the L battalions demolished the fortifications; the dead and ! wounded and the prisoners were transferred from the shore to the vessels in the river; the trophies of war ' were collected; and about four o'clock the magazines of the citadel were fired, and the explosion which followed .laid the stronghold in ruins. Shadows in the valley deepened; night ravenwinged for a while and pitying, softly hid the blight and desola- . tion. Weary heads fell into troubled slumbers, but the sentry, ready and cautious, kept his vigil by the watch . fire.

"The camp-fires flicker out dimly, And exhausted by battle and toil. The battalion in sleep's sweet oblivion Repose on the enemy's soil; But the picket-guard, cautious and wakeful. Are abroad in the gloom of the dell. And the rifles are ready for battle.—ALL'S WELL! At daylight of the 12th, the American force started to embark, and before eight o'clock the last boat had pulled away from the shore. With all the boats of the flotilla in tow, the Mouocacy and Palos steamed down the river, and reached the Bois& anchorage at half-past ten o'clock. Later in the day, the bodies of the two men, killed by the side of the lieutenant, were taken on shore to Boise Island and there buried; the waves of the sea for ever- more chanting their reqUiem. The expedition was ended; whether or not it accomplished the objects for which it was planned the reader can infer from this narrative. But Corea still remains a land of fabled weather and wonders.

- --- The 3rd of July, Admiral Rodgers "passed away with five ships of war that thy." Dispersing. over the silent summer sea, sailing and steaming in company for twenty-four hours, the Colorado, Benicia and Aska steered for Chefoo, while the Mdnocacy and Palos stood away for Shanghai.

The French expedition to Corea was a failure ; the American one was not attended with better results. Who shall penetrate the :seclusion? Away in the misty ages a prince of Corea carried useful ideas into Japan; wader their warrior empress, Jingu, the Japanese sub- jected a portion of Corea.; later, Corean envoys and tribute bearers, diviners, mathematicians, and Bhuddist missionaries arrived in Japan. In 1598 Hideyoshi sent an invading force to Corea, which was everywhere vic- torious; and, to-day, one cannot help pointing to Japan as the country to carry more or less of western ideas of civilisation into Corea. Alone, surrounded by impedi- ments, in 1874, Japan invaded Formosa with her troops, obtained from China admission of her responsibility for the islanders—a measure which the Ministers of Euro- pean sovereigns had failed to obtain—and secured pro- tection for the mariner shipwrecked on the coasts of that dangerous island. Quite recently, by patience and skill, Japan concluded a Treaty of Friendship with Corea, and the supplementary treaty contains an article (X) pro- vided, for the safety of foreigners cast on the shores of Corea. It reads : 'Although no relations. as yet exist between Corea and other countries, yet Japan has, for many years back, maintained friendly relations with them: It is, therefore natufal that in case a vessel of any of the countries of which Japan thus cultivates the friendship, should be stranded by stress of weather or otherwise on the coast of Corea, those on board shall be treated with kindness Ipy Corean subjects; and should such persons ask to be sent back to their homes, they shall be delivered ove,r by the Corean Government to an agent of the Japanese Government residing at one of the open ports of Corea, requesting him to send them back t 6 their native countries, which, requist the agent shall never fail to comply with." Japan is the Sun-land of the Far East, in beauty and utilisation, and many hopeful glances are turned to her promising influence,in the future.

CAPTURE or A SEA Mossxzs.—With great difficulty a sea monster has been captured by some fishermen in Galway Bay. It is gi feet long, about 5 feet in girth, and weighs 'close on three cwt. The mouth is like that of a shark, the upper jaw protruding about six inches beyond the lower. Is addition to this a long pig-shaped snout extends from the upper law about eight inches. The eyes are large and resemble those of a cow. There are five row of gills on each side, divided by a laver of grizzly flesh. There are two ',we of teeth; each tooth is about two inches long asd as thin as* wafer. Each tooth laps over its neighbour. The akin is of a silvery colour, and underneath it is a "umber of spots knows as buttons. These diminish in size as they' near the tail. The tail is fan-shaped. There is no dorsal fin. The buttons are half-an-inch in diameter at the head, and in the centre of each is la thorn a quarter of an inch long as sharp as a needle.

ALLEGED FoßpEux By A DOCTOR.—At Liverpool Police Court. on Saturday, before Mr. Raffles, a gentlemanly-look- ing man named John Wilson°, living in Chadwick Mount, Everton-valley, and described as a doctor of medicine, ap- peared on the charge of having forged, altered, and put off a cheque for £2 with intent to defraud, on the 30th May. Chief Detective-Inspector Marsh prosecuted. It was alleged that on May 26th prisoner called at the shop of Mr. Bowen, clothier, mid ordered a suit of clothes. Two days subse- quently be called again and ordered an umbrella. On the 30th he again called, and after directing an assistant to for- ward his clothes to Chadwick Mount be produced a crossed cheque far £2, and requested Mr. Bowen to cash it. lie said be bad received it from a patient, but as it was crossed he could not get the cash immediately for it. The prose- cutor then gave the prisoner cash for the cheque, which was signed "William F. Denton," and purported to be payable at the Kirkdale-road branch or the North and South Wales Bank. It was afterwards ascertained that no person of that name had an account at the bahk, and that the prisoner had left the city. Prisoner was apprehended in London on June 181.—The prisoner now stated that be got the cheque from a person be knew by the name of Denton,l and that be was ,perfectly innocent in the matter.— Mr. Bafflercommitted him to the assizes for trial, bail ir. two sureties of £25 each being accepted for prisonet's ap- pearance.

DEPARTURE OF EARL SPENCER FROM DUELIN.—At half- past two on Saturday afternoon Earl Spencer left Ireland consequent upon his vacating the seat of Lord Lieutenant. He was accompanied by Couetess Spencer. The whole route from Dublin Castle to Westland Row Railway Station was lined with military and police. Earl and Countess Spencer were cheered as they passed through the streets. Though the cheering on the threshold of the Castle ex- ceeded the hissing, a painful suspense immediately followed, and was then succeeded by a most regrettable incident. The father of the convict Poole, who was executed for the mur- der of the man Kenny, was talking to the crowd in an ex- cited manner, and on catching sight of Earl Spencer and the Countess in their carriage, which was partly closed, he wildly waved his arms about, and, after a wild" boo," cried out "You are the man that murdered my son." The action of Poole attracted the immediate attention of the by- standers, several of whom hooted the Viceroy, who was closely watching the people on each side of him. The hooting, however, Was quickly drowned by a really good cheer, and the carriage passed quickly on. A number of young fellqws, howevrh, followed hissing, and throughout the route there were alternate bursts of cheering and hissing. This mixed kind of farewell continued the whole way to the station. where the Nationalists bad evidently or- ganised a hostile demonstration, for the moment the carriage hove in eight hissinrwas started and cries of "Foxy Jack" and other insulting epithets were used. There was, how- ever large preponderance in sound of hearty cheering. The enthusiastic reception which greeted the earl and his countess inside the terminus made amends for what had occurred outside. Previous to leaving Earl Spencer had held a farewell reception at the Castle. Before leaving the Castle, Earl Spencer conferred the honour of Knighthood on Mr. W. S. B. Kaye, Assistant Under Secretary, and Mr. John Ball Greener, C. 8., Commissioner of Valuation in Ire- land. Prior to his departure.from the capital, Earl §pencer conveyed to the metropolitan police, through their officer, his acknowledgement of their praiseworthy conduct during a trying period in the history of Ireland. He regretted 'hat 'a strike should have occurred among the men during his Viceroyalty, but intimated that the blame was not alto- gether on their aide, as a mistake had been made by the Administration.

CANDIDATES FOR THE NEW CO/STITUENCIES.—The Press Association has issued a revised list of candidates for the various conetituencies of Great Britain, as provided by the Redistribution Act, brought up to Saturday last. From this it appears that the total number of candidates who have al- ready offered themselves or been chosen by the various party associations in Great Britain is 975, of which 795 have appsared ia England 48 in Wales, an". 132 in Scot-. land. 420 Liberals and 375 Coneervatives appear in Ene- laud, 30 Liberals and 18 Conservatives in Wales, and 94 Liberals and 38 Conservatives in Scotland. Of the 443 constituencies into which England is to be divided, 294 are provided with candidates of both parties, 81 with Liberals, 54 with Conservatives, and 10 are unprovided with either. Of the 29 Welsh constituencies, 18 have candidates of both parties, nine have Li'.erals only, and two are unprovided with ei•her ; while of the 71 in Scotland, 33 have c ndidates ot both parties, 31 Liberals only, six Conservatives only, and one neither. 404 members of the present House seek reelection to the new Parliament for constituencies in Great Britain ; 117 Liberal and 33 Conservative ask re-elec- tion for seats they now hold, such seats being unaffected ! by the Redistribution Act; 93 Liberal and 105 Conservative members for their present seats as remodelled by that Act, and 26 Liberal and 20 Conservative members for consti- tuencies altogether unconnected with those for which they now sit, there thus beiteg 246 Liberal and 158 Consarvalive members known to be seeking re-election. Three of the present members are put forward in more than one consti- tuency—Mr. Gladstone, Midlethian and Shipley ; Lord Randolph Churchill, Central Birmingham and North Pad- dington •," and Mr. Bradlaugh, Northampton and East Fins- bury. Twenty-four of the Liberal and six of the Conserva- tive candidates in England are distinguished as labour can- didates, and nine of those in Scotland as crofters. I THE CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT.

NEW GOVERNMENTAL APP3INTMENTS.—The appointments of the Eoglish Law Officers have now been definitively ,nade, Mi. R. E. Webster, Q C.. haring been appointed ti torney-General, and Mr. J. E. Gorsr, Q C., S dicitor- General. Mr. C. Stuart Wortley, the junior member for Sh-ffield, has been appointed Under-Secretary of State for the Horne Department. Mr. G. Downey, M.P. for the North Riding, has accepted the office of Surveyor-General of Ord- nance, which was off-red to Sir W. Btrttelot, but has been declined by him. The Right Ron. Edward Gibson, upon his eqevation to the peerage, will adopt the title of Lord Ashbourne, of Ashtourne, in the county Meath. Lord Henniker and Lord de Roe have been appointed Lords- in-Waiting; and the Duchess of Buccleuch has been appointebl Mistress of the Robes in Her Majesty's House- hold. THE DISTRIBUTION OF HONOURS.—PEERAGES DECLINED. —lt is said that Sir William Harcourt, Lord Richard Gros- venor, and Lord Kensington are to be raised to the peerage The Daily News says :—We understand that the Queen has been pleased to sanction the offer of a peerage to Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P., which that gentleman has thought it right I respectfully to decline. A peerage has also, we are in- formed, been offered to, and declined by, the Right Hon. C. P. Villiers, M.P. Btronercies have been accepted by Mr. B. Jardine, M.P.. and Mr. T. Brocklebank, of Springwood, Allerton. Mr. Watts, ILA., has declined the baronetcy offered him. The Queen has hem pleased to confer the decoration of the Royal Order of Victoria and Albert on Countess Spencer, as a mark of Her Majesty's personal esteem. A baronetcy has been conferred upon Mr. H. F. Vernon. of Hanbury Hall, Worcestershire, and C.D. upon Mr. R. IL Hobart, late private secretary to Lord Hartirgton. THE GOVERNMENT AND MR. BRADLAI7OH.—A corrected edition of the Orders of the Day has been issued for Mon- day. July ath. In this revised list the Government have availed themselves of the privilege of making supply the first order of the day, and the liou.e will accordingly on that night proceed with the Civil Service Estimates. At the commencement of the sitting it is expected that Sir M. Hicks-Beach will mtke a tatement on the policy of the Government, which may give rise to some debate. On the same day also Mr. Bradlaugh will appear and claim to be sworn, and Sir M. Hicks-Beach will move the resolu- tion which has been so of ten proposed by Sir Stafford North- cote.

NORTH LINCOLNETHRE —RESOLUTION TO CONTEST THE SEAT.— the reit in this division rendered vacant by the elevation to the peerage of Mr. Rowland Winn will be con- tested. On Monday a telegram was received in Brigg from Sir H. Meysey‘Thompson, Bart., Kirby Hall, York, the adopted Liberal candidate for the Brigg Division of the county, who is travelling on the Continent, stating that he had decided to come forward in the Liberal interest. The de- cision of Sir LI Meysey-Thoinpson has given the greatest satisfaction to the party. AYLESBURY.—Baron Ferdinand Da Rothschild on Mou- thy issued an address to the electors of Aylesbury as the candidate for the vacancy caused by the elevation of Sir Nathaniel, De Rothchild to the peerage. He advocates the cheapening and facilitating the transfer ef land, equalising the duti, son real or personal estate, the aboli- tion or modification of tke law of entail, local option, and Free Trade. . .

THE New ATTORNEY-GENERLL. Mr. R. E. Webster, Q.C., the newly-appointed Attorney-General, who is contest- ing the seat for Launceston, vacated by the elevation of Sir H. Giffard to the woolsack, addressed a meeting on Satur- day evening. He said he had been charged with advoca- ting a tax upon tea. That was not true, for he was op- posed to any increase of that dutv. Speaking generally, he was against a tax upon sugar, but in the case of the bounty- fed sugar of France, which came in to compete unfairly with sugar of English manufacture, the question arose whether it might not b 3 subjected to some kind of duty without injury to the consumer. He had no obj-c- -tion to revenue being obtained from taxes levied upon spirits. WESTMINSTER. At the first of the Ministerial re- elections on Monday, Mr. W. H. Smith was returned without opposition for Westminster, and Mr. A. J. Balfour for Hertford. _ _

.v. NORTH LEICESTERSHIRE.-0a Tuesday afternoon Lord John Manners addressed a large meeting of Conservatives at Melton Mowbray, North Leicestershire, prior to his re- el( ction as Postroaster-Creneral. The task of the new Gov- ernment was serious, and be would not stats their pro- gramme ; but they had to restore order out of chaos in Egypt, and restore confidence in India.—At a meeting of the Council of the North LPicestershire Liberal Association on Tuesday night it was unanimously decided not to oppose the re-election of Lord J. Manners. .

EYE.-Mr. Ashmead•Bastlett (C) and Mervyn Hakes (R) were nominated on Tuesday. DUBLIN.-Mr. Plunkett, in returning thanks for his un- opposed return for Dublin University, on Tuesday, said he believd the vast majority of his constituents wished him to give his beat support to Lord Salisbury. who had taken ' office at a crisis when affairs at home and abroad were at a deadlock. _

MID-Lnecor.ssmait The nomination took place on Toes lay. Mr. Chaplain and Mr. Stanhope, Conservatives, were proposed by Mr. A. S. L. Melville, and smonded by Mr. R. C. Beigne-Coupland. There being no other nomina- tions received, they were declared duly electel. COUNTY Dows.—Mr. John St. Brown. the Liberal can- didate in opposition to Lord A. Hill, issued his address on Tuesday. The Liberals and Nationalists have coalesced to support him. RE-ELECTIONS —Sir William Hart• Dyke, Chief Secretary for Ireland ; Colonel Stanley, Secretory for the Colonies ; Lord John Manners, Postmaster-General ; and Colonel Walrend and Mr. Sidney Herbert, Junior Lords of the Trea- sury, were on Wednesday re-elected for their respective constitoencies without ooposition. Mr. J. C. Moore Stevens (C) was elected for North Devonshire, thus fillin7 the vacancy caused by the elevation of Sir Stafford Northcote to the p,erage. The polling at Launceston to fill the vacancy caused by the elevation of Sir Harding° G ffard to the woolsack, took place on Wednesday, the candidates being the new Attorney-General (Mr. Robert Webster, Q.C.), and Mr. William Petbick (Liberal). The Attorney-General was returned by a majority of 43 Mr. Pethick polled 40 more votes than the Liberal candidate obtained at the last general election, and the Conservatives polled 22 fewer , than in 1880, when they had a majority of 'lO5. The new , Civil Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. Ashnsead Bartlett, was on Wednesday re-elected for the borough of Eye, the voting being as foliows:—Bortlett, 473; Hawkes (L), 336; or a Conservative majority of 137, as against 62 at the last general election. Both sides polled fewer voles yesterday than in 1880—the Conservatives 67 and the Liberals 142 fewer. A Cabinet Council was held at the official residence of the First Lord of the Treasury at noon on Wednesday, all the members being present except Lord Carnarvon. OPPOSITION TO LORD R. CHURCHILL.

At a meeting of the Liberels at Woodstock, held on Fri- day night, it was resolved to oppose the re-election of Lord R. Churchill, and a resolution wee carried to support Mr. Corrie Grant, of the National Liberal Club, for the vacancy. Mr. Grant's address says that an alliance of landowners, publicans, and Iris') patriots had defeated the Liberal Go- vernment. Lord Randolph Churchill had been prominently before the public, not for the earnestness of his convictione —for apparently he had not yet settled with himself what his political principles were to be ; not for his lofty ser- vices to his country ; but for intrigues against his own ' leaders, his outrages on all decency of (Matt, and the utter- ances of slanderous abuse which he had poured on his opponents. In this crisis he asked the electors to pass sen- tence on him. Woodstock was a dying borough. LI a few weeks it would no longer return its member to Parliament. As a crown to their long historical record, as a proof of their manliness and sincerity, he asked them as an ardent Independent Radical, for their votes, to show their allegi- ance to the great statesman whom their late member had consistently thwarted, traduced, and reviled.—A vote of confidence in Mr. Grant was passed, ad pledging the meet- ing to support him. Lord R. Churchill (Conservative) and Mr. Corrie Grant (Liberal) were duly nominated for the representation of Woodstock on Monday. Both parties at Woodstock are hard at work, and Lady Randolph Churchill has been busily engaged in forwarding her husband's interests. Mr. Grant is being assisted by a number of labouring men and Radicals.

-.,—.-,... Lord Randolph Churchill has issued a supplementary ad- dress to the electors of the borough of Woodstock, in which he says:—" My object in writing to you Ibis further address so tar as I can, to express to me my great concern and regret that it is impossible for me at this rather anxious time to visit your widely-extended constituency and per- sonally support my elaioss. I recognise the great 4isad- vantage accruing to me on this account, but I place the interests of the public service far above any personal in- terest of my own, and I would far rather that the latter than the former should suffer damage. Having never held office before.'it is absblutely incumbent on me to give to the ac- quisition of int rmatton as to the nature and extent of my duties double the time and application which might be necessary for other persons more fortusately situated. You are, moreover, aware that eecently the interests of India with regard to her frantiee security have been specially compli• caod and critically affected. Nor has this state of things altogether passed away. Under 'these circumstances it is impossible for me at this moment to leave London and go among you as has been on former occasion!, my practice and my pleasure." Mr. Corrie Grant is exerting himself to the utmost to make himself known amongst the electors. He attended seberal meetings on Tuesday night, and on the whole was well received. He is being warmly supported by the local leaders of the party, and has received offers of assistance from various Liberal organisations outside the constituency. while numerous letters have reached him from various parts of the country speaking approvingly of his candidature. The Conservatives, though• apparently not exerting, them- selves so strennously as their opponents, are nevertheless actively engaged in Lord Churchill's interest. Mr. Irwin, of the Westminster Conservative Association, who is acting as Lord Randolph Churchill's agent, was busily engaged oa Tuesday in completing the arrangements for ensuring the polling of all Conservative voters. Lady Randolph Church- ill and Lady Carzon continued their canvassing of the electors on Tuesday. Although the constituency is small, the voters are spread over a wide\ area. The borough of Woodstock includes 12 village in addition to Woodstock it- self, with a total population of about 7,000. The number of electors is 1.094. At the last election, in 1880, the popniation was 7,477, and the electori numbered 1,087. Lord R. Churchill then received 512 votes, and Mr. Hall, his opponent, 452. The Conservatives are weakest at

Coombe, a purely agricultural village, with a population of 541. On Wednesday the Dalte of M trlborough drove into Woodstock from Blenheim Palace, had an interview with Lady Randolph at her hotel, and invited her to cake her headquarters at 13ienh,im until the cloiie of the contest. On Wednesday the duke confirmed the report that he had pro- mised to lend his private carriages to convey Lord Ran- dolph's supporters to the ptill ; and Mr. Grant's committee ' is seeking t counteract Las influence by obttining a num• ber of vehicles from the metropolis. Sir. H. Drummond- Wolff address'ng a Conservative meeting in one of the out- districts on Wednesday night, stated that Lord Randolph would be unable to leave his official duties in the present critical state of affairs in India, adding that the Conserva- tive Government was determined VIII, a large piece of I territory should remain between the British and Russian dominions. It was absolutely necessary, he said. that Russia should not be allowed to intrude upon Afghan- istan.
_ HE ALT H, STRENGTH, and ENERGY.

Mr. Edward R. Russell, editor of the Liverpool Daily Post, has accepted an invitation to contest the Brigton Division of Glasgbw in the Liberal interest. An amusing anecdote is told by an old inhabitant of Kinderhook of Thomas H. Benton when the guest of Mr. Van Buren at one of those famous 'dinner parties for which "Lindenwold" was noted in its palmy days. After the dessert had been served' finger-bowls were brought in, and were viewed with some suspicion on the part of one or two of the guests. When dinner was over Mr. Benton said to a friend, "I observed Mr. Van Buren immerse the tips of his 'fingers in one of those little glass bowls and wipe them daintily on his napkin, but I just rolled back my sleeves and took a good, plain Republican wash." • ONE cum of Army and Navy MEDICINES contains suffi. dent to cure contagious disees.s of a certain class (internal or external); Ca 6d., parcels post 58. single bottles of Mixture, 2s. 6d.—METHUEN, operative Chemist (late Bowker). 332, Deansgata, Manchester.—Advt.
MANCITESTEI SHIP CANAL BILL.
MONDAY.

Mr. James Abernethy, C.(., examined by Mr. 'Michael, Q.C.. consulting engineer to the promoters, sdd he had carefully inspected the p 1 ma of Mr. Leaner Waiiarns, and had come to the conclusion that the course of the propesed canal was well designed. There were no engineering diffi- culties connected with the execution of the works. The works would not, in his opinion, injuriouely interfere with the natural action of the tidal ctirrents. If the works had any effect they would be rather beneficial than otherwise to the estuary. What was proposed to he done would not tend to draw the water along the Cheshire side of the river.—The Chairman asked Mr. Bidder, QC., to explain what the contention of the Mersey Dock Board was as to the effect of the proposed works.—Mr. Bidder said their contention was that the works would tend to develop a permanent channel on the Cheshire side welch would operate preju- dicially to the rest of the estuary.—Cross-examined by Mr Pope for the London and North-Western Railway Company, owners of the Gareton docks, witness said that the dredged channel from Bastham to Brotuborough would be maintained partly by scour and partly by dredging. At the close of the witness's evidence, the chairman said he would like couneel for the promoters to direct their fur- ther engineering evidence to the question whether the ab- straction of the water from the estuary would cause damage to the bar, and Le what extent.—Mr. William Shelford, CE., Westminster, who was next examined, explained the general tidal ac ion of the estuary of the Mersey, and said that the quantity of water that would be abstracted would not have a prejudicial effect on the bar.—ln answer to the chairman, witness said that if the eff -ct of the works should lead to the abstraction of 21,• per cent. from the tidal capa- city of the estuary, the effect of that abstraction on the bar would be nil.
