IMPORTANT LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE. On Monday afternoon, the annual meeting of the Mid- lothian Liberal Association was held in the Queen-street Hall, Edinburgh, Lord Roseberry presiding: " 1 Richmond-terrace. Whitehall, June 170, 1885. My dear Mr. Cowan,—! beg you to coevey to the County Association, at its annual meeting on Monday, my hearty congratulations and best wishes. I rejoice that You meet under the presidency of my friend and late colleague Lord Rosebery, who has to play—if his life be spared— an important part in the future politics of the United Kingdom. The battle of the franchise, which formed the subject of our chief anxiety when I met my constituents last autumn has been won, and the Government which had the honour of fighting it for the nation has by the necessary conse- quence of a vote of the House of Commons, been removed from office. Although it has thus happened that a vote of the Representative Chamber has put an end to the late Cabins; I must take this early opportunity of placing on record my deep and grateful sense of the fidelity of the Liberal majerity of 1880 to its trust. It has had to act under difficulties almost wi:hout example, and I can no more forget than I can repay its confidence and kindness. The time has not arrived for me to enter upon-politics at large, either in the way of defence or criticism. Wbatover we may think of the conduct and course of the late Opposition, it has be. come the Queen's Government, and the interests of the Empire are primarily in it hands. I cow look to its future and not its past. My duty is to support and assist it, as far I as I have the power, in doing right, and not to anticipate that it will do wrong. You may rely upon it that the Liberal party numbers in its ranks an abundance of men qualified by knowledge, ability, and vigour of age to exer- cise the neceseary vigilance. I never anticipated in or sine 1880 that I should solicit at your hands, when the exist- ing Parliament bad done Rework, a renewal of the commis- sion that Midlothian generously gave me. Much less, I need hardly add, have I thought of asking a like honour I elsewhere ; but lam not at this moment released from my I duties to the party which has trusted me, and the first of these duties is to use my strongest and most sedulous efforts to prevent anything that cm mar the unity and efficiency of the great instrument which, under Providence, has , chiefly and almost wholly made our country for the last half century. In these sentiments lam quite sure I shall have your approval and co-operation, and that of the association, and I remain, sincerely yours, W. E. GLAD- I STONE."

Lord Rosenatur addressed the meeting at length. Allud- ing to the circumstances connected with the change of Min- istry, be said he believed the new Cabinet would soon have more of a dissolution than they wished, but he also be- lieved that nob 'sly bad any desire to h tress them. As to Mr. Gladstone, he was convinced that it was impossible for him to retire from publit life, even if he wished to do so, land that the very children of Midlothian would go and pull him out of Ms repose. (Cheere.)—A resolution was adopted expressing continued confidence in Mr. Gladstone as the re- presentative of the county, and looking forward with confi- deuce to the return of the Liberal party at the next general election by an overwhelming majority. Mn. OSBORNE MORGAN, M.P.—An open-air meeting was held on Saturday afternoon, uuder th.s auspices of the Dept- ford Liberal Association, for tne purpose of hearing an ad- dress from Mr. L. dhose, the selected Liberal candidate for Deptford. Mr, 0. Morgan, M.P., in supporting the candi- date, referred to the fact that he was the first native Indian gentleman who had ever aspired to win the uff. ages of an English constituency, and said that his election would not only be a newsdeparture in our Parliamentary history, but it would be a memorable epoch in the history of India. The late Mr. Fawcett used to regret that we were obliged to take our knowledge of the wants and aspirations of our Indian fellow-citizens seco Id-hand, more or less coloured by the channels through which it had to pass. That would no longer be the case if Mr. Ghose were elected, as he would be a tangible representative of 200,000,000 of her Majesty's subjects. (Cheers.) Referring to the recent crisis, he said it was idle to tell them that we had arrived at a momentous period in the history of India ; and vet this moment had been chosen by Lord Salisbury to entrust the destinies of that great country in the hands of a young nobleman whose only qualifications for that slice were that he had spent two months' holiday in India, and had very nearly shot a tiger. (Roars of laughter.) He was not afraid the naw Government would reverse the policy of the Gladstone Goveanment. A faramore humiliating pro- cess was in store for them, and, instead of reversing that policy, he expected they would have to swallow it. (Laugh- ter.) They might as well expect to get grapes from thorns as any real genuine progress from the worn-out root of the Tory tree. Ma. J. E. REDMOND, M. t'—At a meeting of the Old- ham branch of the Irish National League, on Saturday, Mr. J. E. Redmond said that the Irish party could view with satisfaction the present political crisis'. The Irish party bad revenged the past, and killed coercive legislation and ad- vanced Home Rule.

Mn. ARNOLD, M.P.—On Saturday night Mr. A. Arnold, M.P., addressed a meeting of the Liberal Council of the northern or Broughton division of Salford, for which he is 1 the accepted Liberal candidate at the General Election. Lord Salisbury, he said, had begun with an apology, and with a curious exhibition of the fact that though his Government II had not the support of Parliament or the people, it enjoyed tbe confidence of Court equerries. It Was a backstairs Gov. ernment. (Laughter.) With regard to the recent Budget, the proper course for the Opposition would have been to at- I tack on going into Committee, or in Committee, those parts of the proposals which they disliked. The reason they did not take that coarse was that they knew well that Mr. Childers would then have succeeded by a large majority in taxing succession to land equally with succession to other property. He believed that just in proportion as Parlia- ment became more democratic it would have a wiser and truer regard for the real interests of Os country. He re- 1 joiced at the change coming over public opinion with re- gard to the government of Ireland. Violent and criminal men were as truly the creatures as the subjects of such a law as that which Parliament established for twelve months in Ireland in 1881. He felt sure there was not a member of the late Government who did not now regard that Act as a serious error. He was in favour of legislation for Ireland according to the views of the majority of her people in re- gard to questions in which the interest which is especially Irish predominated over that which is common to the three countries. THE NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION AND THE NEW GOVERNMENT.—The National Liberal Federation has is •ued a maraifesto on the position of national affairs " constquent on the change of Government brought about by a combina- tion between the Tory party and the followers of Mr. Par- nell." It is stated that an Administration in a minority 'cannot hope to conduct public business with advantage to the nation, whose interests would be held in suspense. If either home or foreign legislation were attempted, the country would be threatened with a constitutional cosflict. The Liberals are warned of the danger to be guarded against in the interval preceding the general election, during which they must be on the watch and be actively preparing. Dangers are to be feared from our foreign relations, especially with regard to Buesia and Afghanistan,•if the views of soma of the leading Ministers were acted upon. What- ever attempts were made to carry out those views should be resisted. The manifesto concludes by insist- ing upon a general election at the earliest time allowed by law.

div.p: TUESDAY.

Mr. J. M. Cunningham, C.E., Edinburgh, examined by Mr. Crepes, said he was consulting engineer to the Caledo- nian Reil way Company, who were the owners of the Firth of Clyde Canal. That canal, which was crossed by swing bridges, was navigated night and day. It was an old canal, and had been open one hundred years. He could not see that there would be any difficulty in working the Munches- ! ter Ship Canal night and d iv. Witness, in further examina- tion, explained the harbour works he bad carried out on ! the Try, and said that the effect of them had been to im- prove the bar from thirteen to fifteen feet. He attributed , that improvement to the embankment which had been made ! directing the flow of the river. Replying Is questions by Mr. Grippe, witness said that he had examined the estuary of the Mersey, acid had studied the plans of the proposed I works to be carried out. He could not see that ! the works would affect in any way the tidal area or the tidal flaw. It was impossible for the low-water channel to be diverted to the Cheshire side, and he thought that the channel from Bromborough to Eistham . locks would only be kept open by continuous dredging.— Mr. Stoney, C.E., and engineer to the Dublin Port and Decks Board, said the proposed canal wes well designed, ! and showed a great deal of engineering, skill on the part of Mr. Leader Williams The works would not have any pre- judicial influence either upon the estuary or the bar at Liverpool. The proposed lock at Eastharn was well situa- ted, and there woad be no difficulty in keeping the gates free from sand —Mr. James Peas, engineer •to the Clyde !Trustees, examined by Mr. Balfour Brown, mid it was pos- sible to deal with the bar at Liverpeol at a moderate cost, las had been done in other rivers. The Clyde had been so improved as to enab'e vessels of the largest tonnage to nevi- gate it.—The Chairman : Do I understand that you have practically made a skip canal to Glasgow ? Yes ; one ,of eighteen miles long. Meseta. Messent, en- gineer to the river Tyne Comrniesioners, and ! Mr. John Fowler, engineer to the Tees Conservancy Corn- , missinners, gave evidence supporting that given by the pre- ! ceding engineers —Mr. G. Hill, CE ,who said that he had ! an intimate acquaintance with the estuary of the Mersey, i extending over a period of thirty years, considered that the abstraction of the water fr !in the tidal flow would be so small that it would be inappreciable.—Mr. Martin, engineer I to the Severn Conservancy Commiesionere, also gave evi- dence in support of the scheme. WEDNESDAY.

Mr. David Cunningham, who has had thirty years' expe- rience as a civil engineer, examined by Mr. Balfour Brown, said he had been engineer to the trustees of the harbour of the Tay for more than fif,een years. A complete survey of the estuary of that river had recently been made by him- self and his assistants. In his view the estuary of the Tay had a rernarkdble resemblance to the estuary of the Merssy. That similatity be- tween the Tay and the Mersey was froni the sea up as far as Runcorn. The position of the harbour of Dundee on the Tay compared in a rein arkable manner with the position of Eastham on the Mersey. In further exami- nation witness said that the proposed works in the Mersey would be beneficial than otherwise to the estuary and the bar.—Crosa-examined by Mr. Bidder : The proposed works would have no injurious effect in making a continuous channel on the Cheshire side of the Mersey. Mr. Alfred biles, M.R. for Southampton, said he was chair- man of the Union Steamship Company, ard had been engineer to the Southampton Docks for forty years. He had given evidence in all the previous inquiries of the ship canal. The abstraction of water by the schema of the pro- moters would, in his opinion, be inappreciable either en the estuary or the bar. About the period of 1884 the making of the docks abstracted 25,000 000 cubic yards of water on a twenty-one foot tide, and the bar was now better than it was then. When they toek 25,000 000 cubic yards from 710,000,000, the total cuhical capacity of the estuary, they got an abstraction of 1-14th (Mr. Bidder : 1.28 th), whereas the abstraction of 272,000 000, the utmost that the plans of the promoters would involve, would only be one in 142 of the total capacity. Ha argued from that that the abstrac- tion caused by the promoters' plans could not cause any appreciable injury.—Mr. J. Wood, steamship broker and shipowner, of West Hartlepool and Swansea, was examined as to the navigation of the canal by vessels of 2,000 and 2,600 tons register. He would prefer sending his ships up the canal to sending them to Garston, and he would not require any extra freight. THURSDAY.

Mr. A. Adamson, naval architect, f )rmerlv with Messrs. Elder, of Glasgow, stated on Thursday that ocean-going vessels, either as new constructed or with trifling alterations ef the masts would be able to pass under the proposed bridges over the canal.—Mr. Wheeler, engineer to the Bos- ton Harbour Commissioners, stated that in his opinion the quantity of water entering the upper estuary would not be aiminished the works connected by the eaanal.—T4 Chairman: Do you say that the flood tide has almost as much scouring effect on the Bar as the ebb tide ? Witness : Almost with the full force of the Atlantic dashing against the Mersey sand hanks This must be scouring action. There was a large attraction of water by the Liverpool Docks, but no injurious effect has followed. The proposed works will not take the channel from the Garston to the Eastham side. In cross-exarnination, the witness observed that all the engineers for the promoters were practical men, and those for the opponents were theorists—but able ones, no doubt. (Laughter.) Mr. Wills, engineer to the Weaver Trustees, said he had known the Mersey intimately for the last 20 years. Ile had been engaged in the construction of the Garston docks, and also of the Runcorn Bridge. • He had lately carried out the con- struction of an important dock at Weston Point. There was a very large net return from the Weaver Navigation, which was paid into the fund of the county of Chester. The salt from the salt district passed down into the Mersey principally through the Weaver Ntvigation. After coal and iron, salt was the largest of British exports. The quan- tity ant from Liverpool was about 1,000,000 tons a year, and was shipped in very large vessels. The Weaver Trus- tees were convinced that the canal would do no injury to their navigation, and they were satisfied with the clauses that had been introlueed for their benefit. Witness went on to state that 54 steam lighters were now employed in carrying and towieg salt down the Weaver. The canal would give great facilities for loading ocean-go- ing vessels with salt. He did not consider the altered gra- dients cau,sed by the canal to the railways was of any con- sequence whatever.—Mr. T. S. Hudson, managing director of the" Hudson Shipping Company," said he had built his latest shin with fidded masts, with a view to navigation on the Manchester Ship Canal. Captain Andrew Pearson, Board of Trade assessor, akc., at Liverpool, said he had had 26 years' experience at sea. The most paving Olass of ships now were from 1 260 to 2,000 tons. From his experience there would be no difficulty in I navigating the proposed canal.—Captain William Waring said he had conainand4cl vessels of 500 to 2,000 tens. There were several very awkward curves in the Suez Canal. The curves in the Manchester Canal were very much better.

William Bart, amackmaster, Yarmouth, was arrested on Thursday night, charged with attempting to murder his wife by cutting her throat, and inflicting serious wounds upon a man named John Andrews. The motiVe alleged is jealousy. The woman is not expected to recover. A jury was empanelled in the London Sheriff's Court, on Thursday, to assess the damages to be paid by Mr. Irving ) Bishop, the thought-reader, for the libel upon Mr. ) Maskelyne published in Truth, for which the plaintiff had obtained a verdict of £lO,OOO damages, upon which a new trial had been ordered. The jury now awarded Mr. Maskelyne MOO. ' PRINCE EDWARD AT CLEETHORPES.—Prince Edward of Wales made a visit on Thursday to Cleethorpes., and Opened" some improvements which the Manchester, Shef- field, and Lincolnshire Itailway have just completed in that rising watering-place. A sea wall has been erected along the ehdre. with an extensive promenade, and another feature in the improvement scheme is the laying out of a fine public garden.- The Prince, who was the guest of the railway company, had a most cordial reception, and in the course of the day received three addressee. IMPORTANT BRTTING DRCISIObT.—A rather important de- cision affecting the operation of the Betting Act was given in the Court of Appeal on Thursday morning by the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Baggalay and Bowen, on an appeal from the judgment of the Lord Chief Justice in the case of Bridger and Savage. The defendant, a turf commission agent, of Lewes, Sussex. acting as the Plaintiff's agent, had won £l3l odd on the Manchester and Warwick races, but ref aged to pay on the ground that the transaction was illegal. The Lord Chief Justice gave judg- ment for the plaintiff, and their lordships now upheld this decision on the ground that although the person from whom the betting agent had won the money might have refused to pay, the agent, having entered into a perfectly legal con- tract with his principal, was bound to hand the amount over to the latter.

There has been a serious explosion on beard the Valiant, now lying in Lough Swilly. After two ine&ctual attempts to discharge a torpedo it suddenly exploded and Injured seven of the crew, two so sariously that they are not ex- pected to recoover. LORD SALISBURY AND DEpRESSED TRAM—OoThursday a letter was received from Lord Salisbury, in reply to one from Mr. James Thompeon, secretary of the Wolverhampton Conservative Association, calling attention to the great dis- tress prevailing in that town owing to depression in trade. The writer pointed out that hundreds of working-meo. once in comfortable positions, aro now walking the etreets unable to get anything to do, and families are on the brink of starvation. Private benevolence has been taxed to the utmost. The mayor has done all in his power, and the board of guardians gone to the utmost limit of the law in granting out-door relitf, and the only resource now open to the men and their families is the workhouse. The writer asked the Government to step in and find some means of temporary relief, or to provide stite-aided emigration. Lord Saliebury, in reply, expresses the pain which the state- ments in the letter have given hint, and begs to assure Mr. Thompson that toe whole question of deprekion in trade, and the consequences arieing tiatrefrom, will s'aextly be carefully considered by the Government.

WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE. On Saturday, the triennial re-union of former students Of the Warrington Training College ST-S held. Toe proceedings , commenced by a service in toe Parish Church at 11-15 a m , the sermon being preached by Dr. Oakley, the Dean of Manchester. A luncheon was afterwards partaken of in I the large room of the Mount School, which was prettily decorated. There were about 300 'Ales and gentlemen pre- sent, amongst those being Archdeacon Darby, who presided. the Dean of Manchester, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn (canon of Liverpool and Vicar of St. Michael's, Huyton), the Rev. W. Quekett (Rector of Watringtou), the Priecipati of the War- rington Training College (the Rev. Morley Stevenson) and Mrs. Stevenson, the Rev. G. Alt ton and Miss 0. Allton, the Rev. H. Gibson Smith, the Rev. P. and Mrs. Slater, the Rev. J. T. Leicester Darwall (Sr. John's, Walton, near Warrington) and Mrs. Darnall, the Rev. J. A. Drummond, the Rev. .1. Watson Watson (Diocesan Inspector), Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Mr. and Mrs. J. R. litaskton, Mr. and Mrs. Pearse, Mies Goddard, Dr. Watkins (Newton-le-Willows). Mr. Mackie, Alderman Webster, Mr. and Mrs. Pugh, Mrs. Williamson, Miss Smith, and Mr. and Mrs. Wood—After luncheon, Archdeacon Deese proposed the toast of the Queen and Royal Family. lie should like to say that at that moment they were, perhaps, tempted all the more heartily to join in giving expression to the totst when they recollected the very signal advantages which they had dur- ing the last few days found in living under a Constitutional monarchy. (Applause.) Great chan4es seemed to be im- pending, and a great change had jus: taken place in the Administration of the country, and it was du% to the wiedom and the great experience of Her Majesty that that change had been brought about. (Applaksea—" God save the Queen" having been sung, Dr. WATKINS proposed the health of the Dean of Manchester, whose first visit that was, but he (Dr. Watkins) hoped it would be only one of many and regular visits to the college. (Hear. hear.)— The DEAN of MANCHESTER responded in appropriate terms. Archdeacon Dauer proposed "Prosperity to the Warring- ton'Trairaing College." (Applause.) The fact that there were so many old students gathered together, and who, he was sure, would be heartily welcomed by those of the staff on the spot, showed that they must have equally with them the prosperity of the college at heart. Ire looking back, as no doubt they did, to the time of their training in Warring- Son, he was sure they would not be insensible ba the advan- tages which were held outto them whilst they were in train- ing. He must not enter at large upon the questions which were perhaps debateable about the education given just now, but as one whose duty it was to see some examina- tions he was ready to own that it appeared to him that the number of examinations was becoming rather excessive. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) As an examiner he would ven- ture to say to all old and present students that he hoped they would ever keep in mind that the prosperity of their schools and the prosperity ef their college was not really to be tested by success in a class list; and don't lot them make success in an examination the end, ' the all, and the chief aim of their work from year's end to year's end. (Ap- plause.) As he heard it expressed two days go, they lived in this system ef education too much under the influence of three words—hurry, worry, and money. (Applause.)— The Rev. M. STevEstsort (principal of the college) re- sponded, and said he was sure that all of them who had listened to the very kind words in which the Archdeacon of Chester—who, as they all knew, was a very kind and true friend of the college—had proposed the toast of "Pros- perity to the College." had felt in th*,ir hearts the echo of the kindness of the words. He was sure that nothing came home mere nearly to the hearts of all of them than the prosperity of their college. (Applause.) Of course he need not say in speaking for himself and his fellow-workers that the chief aim and end of their lives was to do all they pos- sibly could to promote the welfare and prosperity of the college. (Applause.) lie knew from the dear students who were still with them that they loved their college, that they were hippy, and that they wished it prosperity, not only now, but in the future. (Applause.) tie was also perfectly sure that the many past studests they were SO glad to wel- come that day—many of them were unknown to him person. aliy—cherished, and showed by their presence that they cherished, a hearty feeling as well as a desire for the pros- perity of the college in every way. (Applause.) Mr. Stevenson referred to the examinations just concludida which, he said, had passed off satisfactorily ; but they were still more pleased when they found good reports coming in of the work of past students in their respective schools. lie was thankful that the reports they had received lately had been on the whole very favourable, arid there had been no difficulty in finding schools arid places for those who left them from year to year. (Applause.)-1 he Remit of Wartime:non proposed the health of the visitors.—Mr. J. R. BURTON responded, and the proceedings terminated.—The students spent the remainder of the afternoon in games at croquet, &c., on the lawn, music also beiEg provided in the college.
THE BANKRUPTCY OF MR. R. SPANN.

CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS TAKEN. At the Warrington Borough Court on Wednesday, before Aldermen Pickmere and Chan&ley, and Mr. R. Gsrnett, Richard Spann, wheelright, &0., Warring- ton, was charged with having, on the 4th of March, within four months next before the prehentation of a bankruptcy petition, unlawfully and fraudulently re- moved divers of his goods, to the value of Stc) and up- wards, contrary to sub-seciion 5. sectirm ir of the Debtors Act, 1879. Mr. Percy Davieg prosecuted on behalf of the public prosecutor and the Treasury; and Mr. A. Browne defended.

Mr. Davies, in his opening statement, said the case was one of very great importance, and he would tell the bench shortly the history of the proceedings. It seemed that Richard Spann had filed a bankruptcy petition in the Warrington court on the sth March, and a receiving order was granted the same day, under which order the official receiver, Mr. Ridgway, took possesSion of Mr. Spann'a goods and effects. The prisoner wrote out his statement ot affairs for the of- ficial reoeiver on the 9th March, which statement he swore on his oath was correct. Then followed the public examination, under the new Act, of the debtor, at the County Court, on the z9th March, 188 a, and the debtor swore of course that he had disclosed all his estate, and that he had not remove i or sold any part of his goods for the purpo.e of defrauding his creditors. The first meeting of his creditors took place on the Path March, and a composition of as. iii the £ was afterwards accepted by them. That compo- sition was sanctioned by the court on the 3coh April, and the adjudication was after- wards annulled under the new Act, and the receiving order was resciuded, and the creditors were paid eventually as in the It was afterwards found out that that composition arrangement was really ob- tained by fraud, and one of the creditors—the only creditor of any icopert.ince in Warrington, as all the rest of the largo creditors bel ,nged to Manchester and Liverpool and elsewhere—who had the idea that the prisoner ought to have paid more than 45 in thecaused inquiry to be made, and an application was £ made on his behalf for Spann to be adjudicated a bankrupt, on the ground that be had obtained the composition order by fraud. Such evidence came out in the hearing of that appplication, that on the 25th June directions were given that sperm should be prosecuted. He (1)1r. Davies) simply proposed that day to ask for a remand, as the case would require some getting up on the part of the prosecution. Giv- ing a further accdunt of the case, he said that on the 4th March, that was on the day before prisoner filed his petition, a man named Chatrnen, who had been in his employ as a foreman wheelwright, had instructions to remove a large quantity of goods from the premises of the bankrupt, and he, along with a blacksmith of the name of Bridge, removed a great quantity of material in the, shape of articles used by wheelwrights to different placis up and down the town. A great quantity was removed to Mr. Cross's, wood turner, Rome and Crown-yard, another quail. tity to Mr. Joseph Ashton's, Brici.re Inn, and more to Mr. Clarke's, Royal Oak Branch, Latchford. That was done the day before the petition was signed, and the bankrupt swore in his statement to the official receiver that nothing had been removed or sold within four ~maths of faa bankruptcy, both his statement of affairs and the statement made at his public examination being in. correct and in fact perjury. On the 17th March, which was the day but one before prisoner's public , examination, the same man, Cbatman, and a boy who was an apprentice to Spanu were upon his premises then supposed to be in the hands of the official re- for, some purpose or other, although the goods were ceiver, and everything being under lock and key. It seemed according to Chatman's statement he was sent on to the premises on the night of the 17th and he stayed there till the next morning doing something which he explained was to take up the floor of the paint room, and to remove a quantity of materiel, t ;de paint, •r This was removed from the floor and was hidden in Put down. at the value of £5O. about the premises. other parts of the vremises. nsagliatso the prosecution's own witness, that was a mistake as this Mr. Davies, resuming, said there had been many statements of Chatman's which were supposed to be incorrect, but which had been proved to be eubstaa- tially correct. _ _ material, edir;Br,airba°u3cot

MR. GLADSTONE has addressed a letter to his constituents, which was read at the an- nual meeting of the Mid-Lothian Liberal Association, held in Edinburgh on Monday. It is an important communication, but it is not a political manifesto in the full sense of that term. It is eminently characteristic of the noble statesman who was not to be en- nobled by the gewgaw of a peerage. It is guarded in expression, for Mr. GLADSTONE knows that his lightest word is weighed, but at the same time it reveals a generous spirit—alike to friend and foe. The electors are reminded that the battle of the Franchise which formed their chief anxiety when he last met his constituents has been won, and that the Government which had the honour to fight for it has :since been removed from office by a vote of the House of Commons. This is a plain historical statement, but bow much it . implies! Events have crowded upon each other so rapidly that it is difficuit to realise that Mr. GLADSTONE—but a few months ago—was engaged in a life and death struggle with the House of Lords. He had it in his power at that moment—so strong was the current of public feeling—to give the death blow to the Upper House, and in view of all that has happened, and is likely to happen, we can scarcely help wishing that he had struck when the opportunity was given him. It was due to. his.extiaordinary tact, foresight, and conciliation that the Peers were brought upon their knees, and the way onened which has permitted of the pas- sage of the greatest measure of reform of modern times. If he had done no- thing more than carry the Franchise Bill, and the eats Bill, he would have rendered an incalculable service to humanity ; and we cannot but think that, when the time comes, the Two Millions whom he has enfranchised will show that they are neither forgetful nor ungrateful. Notwithstanding the fact that the fall of the late Government was due to the negligence of soldiers who were not at hand to respond to the bugle-call of their commander, Mr. GLADSTONE—speaking of the party as a wnole—places upon record his " deep and grateful sense of the fidelity of the Liberal majority in adhering to its trust." It is in a similar Catholic spirit that he refers to "the late Opposition" which " has now be- come the Queen's Government." His duty is to support and assist it, as far as he has the power, "in doing right,and not to anticipate that it will do wrong." But the chief interest in the letter is in the reference which is made to the possibility of his continuing to lead the Liberal party. If Woodstock were voting 'iunder an extended franchise, and without re- gard to the territorial" screw," there could be . no question as to its veidict ; for it is noto- rious that it is the working-men of the ' place, who have been loudest in demand- ing that his lordship should not be re-elected without opposition. They have not forgotten, as the Secretary of the Wood- stock Liberal Association observes, that "Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has gone out of his way to court nototiety by slandering the working-men, who foim much the largest portion of his own constituency ;" or that "he has persistently vilified Mr. GLADSTONE in language fit only for Billingsgate." It might have been added that he has slandered not only Mr. GLADSTONE, but almost every other statesman—abusing friends as well as foes—and that he has shown himself in this respect so reckless and unscrupulous as to be a disgrace to public life. What a farce it is to witness such an upstart at the India Office professing to be so anxious abut " frontier security" as to be unable to spare time to pay a visit to Woodstock! Is it not rather that he prefers to avoid the ghosts of his past speeches ? But he cannot escape the consequences of his evil utterances; he will have to lie on the bed that he has made, and it is no bed of roses.

THE Liberals of Woodstock have done the right thing in compelling Lord RANDOLPH CHIJEcHILL to fight for his seat upon, his be- coming a member of Lord SALISEVRY'S Go- vernment. It is time, we grant, that an end was put to the practice of appealing to the electors upon the acceptance of office under the Crown; but, so long as it is open to con- stituencies to express opinion in this way, it is fitting, at any rate, that it should be done in such a case as that of the member for Woodstock. AN ORANGE LODGE named "07, Peace with Honour" was inaugurated on Monday evening in Holy Trinity School, Runcorn. The officers are Brothers W. J. Rankin, W.M. ; E, Jones, D.M. ; S. Leach, W.T.; Bebbington, pro tent. FAITH HEALING AT WIDNES.—The Rev. J. W. Wood, of Port Adelaide, on Sunday held services in Lacey-street schoolroom, and in the Star of Widnes Lodge room, in which he expounded upon the subject, of faith healing, to large congregations. He laid great stress on the efficacy of prayer, and related several marvellous ,cures effected by the faith healind process. He had himself been cured of dyspepsia after having spent a large sum with the doctors to no purpose. ArracKED EY A HORSE AT WIDNES.—On Tuesday evening, while crossing the field behind Mi. Daniel Flo, s,ei residence in Peelhouse-lane, Mr. W. H. Kershaw, timber merchant and builder, was attacked by a mare accompanied by a foal. She made many attempts to kick him, but luckily he evaded her heels. At last, however, she turned round and bit him on the forehead, inflicting a wound from which blood flowed freely. Mr. Kershaw then man- aged to get away, and had his injuries attended to. BRUNSWICK SUNDAY' SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The anniver-

airy sermons in aid of this school were preached in St. Paul's Church on Sunday morning arid evening by the Rev. Jariees Hind. The choir assisted by a large number of scholars sang spscialiy selected hymns and anthems at each service in an admirable manner. jo the evening the" chorus " was given in fine style. On Monday evening the Rev. Charles Garrett occupied the pulpit. There were large congregations at each service and the collections amounted to over £65, A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. W. Betakes and Captain C. W. Hazieburst, at Runcarn Police Com t, on Tuesday, Alice Hampton. an "unfortu- nate," was chaiged with frequenting the stables of Fred- erick Rowles, Brook-street, for an unlawful purpose. Ar a quarter past eleven the woman was found on the premises. and at the request of the prosecutor she was removed by P.C. llammersley. She had been previously found there under suspicious circumstances., She was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. PPOPOSED CEidEIERY FOR HALTON.—For some months the inhabitants of Halton have had under consideration the necessity and advis.hility of providing a cemetery for the township and surrounding neighbomr.,ood. The ran-payers in meeting assembled have now resolved to purchase a burial ground, and have formed a Burial Board cansistiog of the following gentlemen :—The Rev. J. Luckwooel, vicar; Messrs. J. Rutter, H. Lowe, J. W. Haddock, R. Hughes, J. Barrow, and J. Looker. The Board is em- powered to borrow on the security of the rates a sum not i exceeding 400 to be repaid in 30 years. RUNCORN Pianist CHURCIL—The animal servicss in behalf of the National School took place in the Parish Church on Sunday. The pulpit morning and evening was eccupied by the Rev. Canon Morris, D.E., chaplain to hie grace the Drake of Westminster, who preached to large con- gregations. In the afternoon a children's service was held, the Rev, R. Edwards, curate in charge of Newtown Mission Church, delivering an appropriate a iclresa. The choir, augmented 'he 24 girls from the Sunday school, rendered the choral portion of tha servicss in a manlier which re- flected great credit upon Mr. Johnson, the orgauist and conductor. Toe coronation of her Maj:sty the Cjosen was celebrated by the singing of the anthem " Zadok the priest," and the " Hallelujah chorus." The collections amounted to i:.31 19s 33.

For the second time within five years the workmen decided upon a visit to 1314ckpool, mid on Saturday morning, with their sweethearts and wives, they departed for that popular water- ing-place in two special trains. The total number of excur. sionists was 1200.. The works bend accompanied the party. PRIZE FIGHT AT Waniza.—Before Mr. H. S. kraal 1 and Mr J Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Wil- liam Connor, of Midwood-street, and William Kelly, of Milton-road, were charged with committing a breich of the peace by fighting. and Thomas Kelly and Peter McCabe with a similar offer,ce by shouting and making a disturb. ance. It appeared that about three o'clock on the afternoon of the 19th tit, P.C. Almond was in plain clothes, and dis- covered Connor and William Kelly fighting in a field at Crow Wood. They were stripped to the skin, and the ar- rangements were quite on the "professional scale." Seconds with sponges had their positions, and a crowd of about 40 persons formed a ring. The constable watched the men fight about eight or nine rounds, and the disputes and up- roar was so great occasionally that he excted to see the fight end in the" Lancashire fashion," with the use of clogs. Thos. Kelly. McCabe and other persons were shouting and en- couraging the combatants.-McCabe stated he came upon the scene unexpectedly, and was simply a spectator. He seemed aggrieved that other persons were not in the defend- ant's dock beside him.—Superintendent Barker. said he would-have summoned all tbo persons if he couL4 have got their names, but they ran away when they saw the con- stable. He handed in a list of °Tuxes against McCabe and Connor.—Each defendant was b and over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each or 14 days' imprisonment. A warrant was issued for the apprehension 0 Patrick McCabe, and the summons against George Hewitt was returned.

SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WIDNES —Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest at the Simms Cross Hotel, Widnes, on Monday, on the body of John Edwardson, a painter and plumber, who lived at 44, Midwood-street. The deceased poisoned himself on Friday afternoon. It appeared from the evidence that on Saturday, the 20. h ult., the de- ceased went hems and Tired his wife 17s as nis weekly wages. She knowing that he earned much more than this refused to accept the proffered Bum, aud a quarrel ensued. During the disturbance he struck her, and she went in search of a canstable. In her absence the deceased thrashed his mother-in-law, whom be disfigured with a black eye, and then left the house. He did not return until Monday, and after a short stay again departed and did not put in an appearance until Thursday. In the meantime Dr. Cooper, who was in attendance upon the mother-in-law, took out a summons against him for committing the assault. On Thursday the deceased called into the laboratory at Messrs. Dtnis's Copper Warks, and asked Mr. Walter Brown if the liquid he was using would poison anybody. Brown replied that he did not think so. Oa Friday afternoon Fred Harper, a workman at the Copper Manufactory, saw the deceased lying on his back in a field behind the works. He shouted, " Help me, I have poisoned myself." Harper asked him how he had done so, and he answered, " With a bo•tle," but did not rnention the liquid he had taken. A bottle was found buried in the earth near where he was discovered. Mr. Brown was of opinion that the deceased had drank some liquid out of a tank in the yard containing sulphate ot copper and acid.—Dr. McLennan deposed that when he saw the deceased on Friday afternoon he was black about it' month and teeth. There was some vomit near where be was found and be examined it. It appeared to have come from a corroded stomach. In his opinion the deceased had taken an irritant poison, but he was ntiable to say what it w without making a post nwrtent examination—Tee Coroner having review,d the evidence, the jury returned a verdict to the effect that Edwardson com nitted suicide whilst tem- porarily insane.

ASSAULT ON A lanu, AT WESTON.—Kate Ritchley, a married woman, living at Weston, was summoned to Run- corn Petty Sessioos on Monday for assaulting Margaret Farrell, 14 years of age. It appeared that on Monday evening, the 22nd ult., Farrell and several companions were walking through the village when the defendant's daughter asked them if they had "seen their chaps," and used other irritating language. The daughter then kicked the com- plainant, and pulled her about the hair. Subsequently the defendant came epon the scene, seized the complainant by the throat, and knocked her to the ground. A COUNTY COURT FOR WinNES.—The solicitors in St. lidens are moving to have the county court held there at more fiegitect intervals than once a fortnight as at present, and a petition signed by them is being placed before tbe inhabitants for approval, and will be presented to the Lord. I NONCONFORMISTS AND UNIVERSITY HONOURS.— The Liberator says :—" In 1882 we were able to state that, in as many as fifteen years out of twenty- three, the Senior Wrangler at Cambridge had been a Nonconformist. This year, also, the Senior Wrang- ler is a Nonconformist—Mr. Berry, of King's. Mr. Jessop, of Clare, is the son of an Independent min- ister. In Part I. of the Classical Tripos, the first class contains the names of Mr. Conway, of Caius, the son of an Independent minister, and of Mr. Rouse, of Christ's, son of a Baptist minister. Mr. G. E. Green. the Senior of the Historical Tripos, ,is a Congregationalist. In the Law Tripos, Mr. Kerly, of St. John's, who is bracketed Senior, is a 'Nonconformist. Among the ladies who have dis- tinguished themselves, and who belong to Noncon- formist families, are Miss Case, of Girton, who is in the first class in the second part of the Classical Tripos; Miss Silcox, of Newnham, first class in Part 11. of the Classical Tripos; and Miss Rickett and Miss Hewett, who rank as Wranglers. We do not profess to give a complete list; these names are sufficient to show that, when Nonconformity has fair play, it can hold its own with Church of Englandism in the matter of culture. And for generations past it has not had fair play." VALUE OF FREEHOLD FARMS IN SOUTH LANCA- SIIIRE.—Mr. J. B. Leach, of the firm of J. B. and B. Leach, of St. Helens and Liverpool, submitted to public auction on Tuesday afternoon at the Royal Hotel, Prescot, to a large company of local gentle- men., the valuable estate situate in the township of Whiston, and known as the 4' Royal Oak Estate," and comprising two farms called the "Royal Oak Farm" and Shaw-lane Farm," containing respec- tively 100 a Or Bp, and 26a 3r 19p of choice land, in a high state of cultivation, with excellent farm houses and outbuildings, flourishing brickworks, and 15 cottages, smithy, and wheelwright's shop. After the auctioneer had referred to the special value resting in farm property in this part of the country, through the prospect of the land being re- quired for building purposes, and to their high state 'of cultivation, recommending this class of invest- ment as of the safest kind to be found, he received a first offer of £9.00, followed by £lO,OOO, £ll,OOO, .£11,500, £12,000, and resulted in a sale being effec- ted to Captain R. R. D. A. Willis, J.P., of Halsnead ' Hall, Whiston, at £13,500. Messrs. Maxstead and Gibson, of Lancaster, were the vendor's solicitors. RE-ELEcTION OF SIR RICHARD CROSS.—The formality of re-electing Sir Richard Assheton Cross to the representation of South-West Lancashire, in ' consequence of the acceptance by him of the office 1 of Home Secretary in the newly-formed Cabinet, took place on Tuesday at St. George's Hall, Liver- , pool, no opposition being offered by the Liberal party of the division to the nominee of the Conser- vatives. Mr. Wilson, acting 'Under Sheriff fdr the County, was the returning officer, holding his court in the Sheriff's Court, where, at the appointed hour , of twelve, there were present Sir Thomas Edwards- Moss, Messrs. Gilbert Winter Moss, T. Stanley Rogerson, Marcus Brown Westhead (Newton), and Woodnorth (secretary to the South-West Lancashire Conservative Association). The time fixed for the receipt of nominations was from twelve noon to two p.m., but of course it was well known that no ! opposition was intended, and the whole proceedings therefore were merely of a routine character, no in- terest being taken in them at all. At the appointed hour of twelve the following nomination was handed in :—Sir Richard Assheton Cross, G.C.8., Eccle Riggs, Broughton-in-Furness, Lancashire (Conservative). Proposed by Sir Thomas Edwards- Moss, Otterspool, Garston ; and seconded by Thomas Bland Royden, 8, Mossley 11111-road, Aigburth, Garston. Among the electors of the division who subscribed their names to the nomination paper as assenting voters were—William Pilking,ton, Roby Roby; Edward Banner, Blacklow House, Roby; and John Birch all, The Oaklands, Rainhill. Sir Richard Cross was nominated a second time, his proposer in the second nomination paper being Arthur Bower Forwood, The Priory, Woolton Hill road, Little Woolton; and his seconder Marcus Brown Westhead, Newton-le-Willows. The second paper was also signed by eight assenting voters; but as the first was, after examination by the pre- siding officer, declared formal and valid it was not presented. After an interval of two 'hours, in ' which, of course, no objection had been taken to the nomination paper, and no opposition offered, the returning officer declared Sir Richard Assheton Cross, M.P., K.C.8., the duly elected member for South-Western Lancashire.

fGREAT FALL IN THE PRIOR OF CHESHERN CMIESE.—At Nantwich cheese fair, on Thursday, there was an immense pitch of Cheshire theese, over ninety dairies being on offer, and weighing quite fifty tons. Trade was exceedingly dull; and, ' in order to effect sales, a reduction in prices below those current last month had to be taken of lOs per cwt. No such sweeping fall as this has taken place in the price of Cheshire cheese for many years. THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.—At the quarterly meeting of the Manchester and District Committee of the Liberation Society, held at the offices, St. James's-square, Manchester, on Tuesday, Mr. Samuel Knowles in the chair, a resolution was unanimously passed, on the motion of Mr. Jesse Bryant, J.P., seeonded by Mr. Edward Cooper (Blackburn), re- cording the committee's • appreciation of the steps taken by the late Government in the direction of religious equality. Approval was also expressed of Mr. Hopwood's intention, on a suitable opportunity, to test the present opinion of the House of Commons on the injustice and inutility of the oath now re- quired from members of Parliament. GRADUATING WITH HONOURS.—'WQ are glad to learn that Mr. F. R. Roberts (youngest son of Mr. Richard Roberts, of 19, Bridge-street, Warrington), a student of Owen's College, and Sharrock Fellow of Lancashire Independent College. Manchester, has just passed the final examination for the degree of Bachelor of Arts of Victoria University, Manches- ter, in the Honours School of History being placed in the second-class. The degree was conferred on Monday last. Article 39 of the University Statutes Provides that any student graduating in the Hon.. ours Schools shall receive at the end of three years from the date of such graduation the further degree of Master of Arts without examination. Mr. Rons • will therefore receive his M.A. degree in 1888. AN EARLESTOWN COLLIER SENT TO GAOL.—Thos. Down, a collier, belonging to Earlestown, was charged before the Warrington magistrates on Thursday with having been drunk in Dial-st. on the previous evening, and also with having assaulted an old man named James Kipling, a lodging-house keeper. Kipling said that on the previous evening the prisoner, who was drunk, was running after two lads, who ran into his house for protection. Prisoner rushed in after them, and as he evidently was going to ill-use them he (Kipling) interfered, whereupon tile prisoner turned upon him, knocked him down teice, and butted him with his head. Prisoner professed not to remember anything that had occurred. He was sent to gaol for seven days without the option of a fine.

THE CLIFTON HALL COLLIERY EXPLOSION.— The following communication appears in a Liverpool contemporary:—" Sir,-1 have read the • extraor- dinary statements' as to ventilation made by wit- nesses at the inquest on the bodies of the 177 men killed j.n the Clifton Hall Colliery. Having had forty years' experience in mining, and been in ten explosions myself, I should like, through the median* of your valuable columns, to ask Mr. Dickenson, Her Majesty's Inspector of Mines whether he con- siders that three seams of coal or Mines, mines can be ventilated by one down-cast shaft, where there are 350 workpeople down at one time, and winding 1,000 tons of coal per day up the same shaft?--- Yours, &c., JOHN Cnoss, mining engineer, 15, Cor- poration-street, St. Helens, June 30:' SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AT PENEETH,-The 411-, nual anniversary sermons in connection with the Penketh Wesleyan Sunday Schools were held at the Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, when two powerful sermons were preached, morning and evening, by the Rev. T. E. Ham, of Birmingham. There were good congregations. Special hymns were sung by the scholars and teachers in a very creditable man- ner. In the afternoon a service of song, entitled "Israel in the Wilderness," was rendered, the con- nective readings being given by Mr. E, Parker with good effect. The chapel was crowded, and the various pieces of music were well rendered. Mr. James IV atson ably conducted, and Miss Helen Garnett presided at the organ with her usual abilitST. The total collections amounted to the hand- some sum of £2l. • .

THE HOME InoN TRADE. -There is no change-rot. - the better in the English iron market. The turn of the tide for which makers of pig-iron have been waiting so patiently and so long appears to be as far off as ever. The Glasgow warrant market has been very flat this week, and little new business is being transacted. Scotch makers find iron difficult of sale, I even though they quote prices which, in comparison with warrants, are extremely low. Closing quota- ; tions of warrants on Wednesday were 40s 9id cash land 40s 101 d a month with sellers, buyers offering one halfpenny per ton less. In the North of Eng- land the pig-iron trade has been still more depres- sed, inquiry being very restricted, while prices are lower. They are being gradually forced down, and No. 3 is now regularly quoted by the merchants at , 325, although the makers who are fairly sold ask 6d per ton more. No 4 forge is 31s 9d. BAILIFF T SANKEY.—At the War- rington County Sessions, on Wednesday. Joseph Souter was charged with having assaulted Samuel Boyle, on the 13th June, at, Sankey. Mr. Worsley i Prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. From the opening statement of Mr. Worsley, it appeared that the complainant was employed as a bailiff by Mx.. , Worthington, sherifCs officer, Wigan. On Satur- day, the 13th June, he had handed to him by Mr. Worthington an authority signed 17 Messrs. Dunn I Brothers, Manchester, authorising him to enter into , possession of premises at Sankey occupied by ; Messrs. William Lo.ngshaw and Son, chemical mann- I facturers. Following.out the authority he went to , Sankey on the same day with the sheriff's officer's clerk, named Berry. Berry entered the premises, and afterwards brought in Boyle, whom he left , there. Later on in the day the defendant, who is Messrs. Longshaw and Son's foreman, entered, and,. seeing Boyle, asked him what he wanted there.. ' Boyle stated his business and exhibited his autho- rity, but defendant ordered him to leave, and as he refused to do this Seater struck him on the neck, and afterwards violently dragged him to the outer door and threw him into the road. Hoyle then went to Wigan, and, having reported the matter, was directed to take out a summons. Mr. Browne, ifl. defence, disputed the right of the complainant to be on the premises under the mortgage for -C2,500 and interest, as the first instalment of that' mort- gage was not due until December. Ile. argued that therefore the magistrates' jurisdiction was ousted. The Bench, however, decided that though they bad nothing to do with the question of right, it was within their province to consider whether an assault had taken place or not. The defendant was then called, and denied that he had used the violence alleged. He had simply carried the complainant,. who was a little man, out of the premises The Bench decided that an assault had been committed,- and imposed a fine of lOs and costs on Soutar. A , comter-summons was dismissed.

SCHOOL TREAT.—On Monday afternoon the children of the Congregational Sunday School assembled at the church in Aseinall-street at about two o'clock, and with banner and II igs marched to a field kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. W. tioldsworth, of Yew Tree Farm, Eccleston. They numbered 150, and were accompanied by the Rev. J. John- son, Mr. Powriell, Mr. Haigh (secretary), and the teachere. On arrival at the held a hymn was sung, and they then. dis- persed to amuse themselves with various outdoor games until four o'clock, when they re-assembled on the lawn, where elaborate preparations lead been made for them, Ad a sumptuous tea was partaken of. Subsequently the pastor, teachers, and friends were entertained. The rest of the day, to nine o'clock, was spent in racing and contests of various kieds for prizes. The doe weather contributed to the general enjoyment. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Goldsworth, and each se.holar received a present of cake and nuts on leaving.—The old chapel building, which has been nerd by the Sunday school since the erec- tion of the new church, is now undergoing repair and alter- ations. The gallery is to be divided into class-rooms. This week, on removing some paneling, some clans-books were I discovered which were in use between 40 and 50 years ago. At a meeting of Oldham cotton operative' on Wednesday evening, at which 1,500 persons are said to have been pre- sent, a resolution was passed to strike rathar than submit to a reduction of 10 per cent THE LORD FREDERICK CAVENDISH STATUE AT BARROW. —The statue of the late Lord Frederick Cavendish, erected in the Town Hall-square, Barrow, was on Tuesday afternoon unveiled by Earl Spencer, the former colleague of the de- ceased nobleman, and until a few days ago Viceroy of Ire- land. The ceremony was most impressive, and was wit- nessed by some thousands of Spectators, many of whom had come long distances to be present. Fortunately the weather was in every respect favourable, and • everything passed off in the most satisfactory manner possible. The statue is regarded in Barrow as a perfect likeness of the de- ceased nobleman to whom the town owes so much of its prosperAy, and whose tragic and untimely death created in it a profound and universal sorrow. The statue, which is in bronze, is the work of Mr. A Bruce Joy, and re- presents the deceased nobleman in his familiar Inverness cape. TnE CONSERVATIVE CLUE BILLIARD HA.NDIOAP'.—The billiard handicap which has been in csurse of competition at the Conservative Club, Earle-street, during the last three weeks, was brought to a conclusion on Tuesday even- ing. In the fifth beats J. Harrison (35 start) beat W. Slinn (40) by 18 points ; and D. Hughes (25) twat T. Kinrade (50) by 23. The final heat between Harrison and Hughes was viewed with some interest. Hughes defeated his op- psnent, and thus won the first prize, a cue and case, presen- ted by Messrs. Orme and Son, of Manchester ; J. Harrison got the second prize, 83; and T. Kinrade and W. Slims each received a prize of 3s 63.

ALLEGED NEGLECT OF A FAMTLY. —Fleury Morris, a wheelwright employed at the Viaduct Waggon Works, Earl estown, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, for neglecting to support his wife and five children, wher,by they became chargeable to the Leigh Union.—The defendant, who pleaded not guilty, was represented by Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens.—Mr. Andrew Ecctestes, relieving officer for the Leigh Union, stated that the defendant was in receipt of 318 per week. On the 28th May the wife applied for relief to the Leigh Union. stating that her husband had turned her out and refused to support her. The Gu rdians allowed her 103 per week, and ordered proceedipgs to be taken against the defendant. The total amount paid up to the present was £2 103. He bad previously written to the de- fendant telling him that his wife had applied for relief, but

the defendant took no notice of the letter. After the Guar- dians had made an order for relief he sent the defendant another notice, and the defendant then wrote stating that he had a house ready for his wife to go to any time she wished. On the receipteaf that letter the relief was stopped and she was told to go and live with him. She did go but the result was that she wan again turned out, and her cloth- ing was sent after her.—ln reply to Mr. Riley, witness ad- mitted that the wife had summoned her husband for assault- ing her in Febraary last, and the case was dismissed by the magistrates, who recommended the wife to go home and act more like a wife.—Mr. Riley considered there was on Case for him to answer, and prged that the Guardians :11)uld have adopted a more humane an reasonable course in pro- ceeding against the defendant, who should have been sum- moned upon an order to pay so much per week, and not under a section which, if convicted, the defendant would be committed to prison ae a rogue and vagabond. The defen- dant had written to the Guardians stating that he had the house door open for his wife and children when they chose to COMP, but her relations had. persuaded her to go away, and they must keep her while she was away. He hoped the magistrates would dismiss the case, and give the wife an opportunity of returning to her home—The Bench said the Guardians had another caurse open to them, and that was to seek an order for the defendant to contribute to the sup- port of his family, and they considered that that was the proper course. There was no evidence to prove that the , defendant was an idle man, and they believed be was an in- dustrious man. There appeared to have been some mistake as to the manner in which the case had been brought before them, and they were of opinion that the Guardians should merely have applied for an order of support. Under those circumstances they dismissed the case.—The Clerk observed that the Guardians would still have power to apply for an order in case the defendant failed to maintain his wife and family.
A COLLIERY MANAGER HEAVILY FINED.—COL. McCORQUODALE, J.P., ON COLLIERY EX-

PLOSIONS. At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Col. MeCorquodale, Mr. R. Houghton, Mr. I'. J. Gilleepie, and Mr. W, F. Gooch, a case of great importance to colliery pro- prietors and managers was heard. Jams Newton, the cer- tificated manager of Collins Green Colliery, was summoned for an offence against the Coal Mines Regulation Act. The proceedings were taken by Mr. Henry Hall, the Government inspector of mines for the district, and Mr. Collins, solici- tor, Liverpool, appeared to prosecute. The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens.—Mr. Collins said he had been instructed by the Treasury to prosecute the defendant for an offence against the Bth rule of the special rules in force at Collins Green Colliery. The 8:11 special rule was to the effect that imme- diately before any shot in a mine was fired # competent person, appointed for the purpose, must examine the place and the places contiguous thereto, and he must not allow a shot to be fired unless it is safe so to do, and the shot ;mast only be fired by a competent person appointed for that purpose. He (Mr. Collins) thought that was one of the most important sections of the whole Act, dealing as it did with explosions of gunpowder in mines where inflam- mable gas had been found. Collins Green Colliery was a mine in which inflammable gas had been found, and it was most important, therefore, that that rule should be strictly adhered to. There was a shot lighter named Myers, whose duty it was to fire shots, and before shots were tired to ex- amine the place and be satisfied that it was safe for shots to be fired. As a matter of fact a collier named Parr had been in the habit of firing his own sbots without any such examination at all, thereby committing a clear breach of the rule. Under the 3191 general rule the manager was re- sponsible, and in the 60th sectien of the Act the penalty was fixed at not exceeding £2O —Mr. J. 0. Swift said the Col- lins Green Colliery Company had been opening up a new mine, and the mine with respect to which that information had been laid was one called" Potato° Del ph," which had been opened during the present year. It had only been proceeded with a very short distance, and about 20 men were working in it: Inflammable gas, it was true, had been found in the mine, but it was only in such small quantity as was prac- tically found in every mini in process of being opened out. The company had appointed a shot lighter named John Thomas Myers in February last, and the defendant James Newton, the certificated manager, who had had 25 years' ex- perience, found Myers a competent person to fire shots. He thought everything was going on in apparent safety, and he bad no reason to suspect that any shot firing was being done by any other person whatever except by the duly ap- pointed shot lighter. Unfortunately he subsequently found that a collier named John Parr had fired his own shots with the knowledge of Myers, the shot lighter. Parr was the only man who had fired shots with the exception of Myers, who had failed to report it to Mr. Newton. It was with- out the latter's consent or knowledge that there was any breach of the rules, and he held that a nominal penalty would meet the justice of the case. He added that since the offence Myers bad been discharged, and was found work in another part of the mine, and another competent man appointed in his place.—After a consultation with the other magistrates, the Chairman said : James Newton, we have heard the two gentlemen who have spoken, and we have received full information upon this subject. Of course you are well aware in inflicting a fine here we do not do it solely fer the purpose of punishing you, but as a warning to others. We have bad terrible colliery accidents in this district in which a great number of lives have been lost, and within the last few weeks you have read of a very seri- ous accident which caused the loss of a great number of lives. It is opt' duty to sit here and warn all in authority like tourself to exercise the greatest possible core, knowing the important' responsibilities upon men in your position and we cannot help cocsidering the Act is laid down so clearly before Us. We want to make a warning to those who are like yourself in such positions, and you will be fined in the sum of £5 and costs. •

div.head: ANTI-VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: ANTI-VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS.

Before Colonel George McCorquodale and Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch at the New- ton Petty Sessibris on Saturday, John Blower, of &ries-. town, was summoned for disregarding a magistrates' order to have his two children vaccinated.—Mrs. Blower appeared, and said she would admit that the children had not been vaccinated when the summons was received, but they had been vaccinated on the previous Thursday morning by Dr.. Patterson.—Mr. Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer: If that is true I must aek that the case be adjourned until next court day to see if it is true.—Mra. Blower then banded to the Bench a letter to the effect that the parent did not ob- ject to vaccination, but they had been waiting for calre rawer. The eldest child had not been well from birth. The letter was Signed " Yours sincerely, Dr. Patterson."— The Clerk asked if Dr. Patterson had written, that letter.— Mrs. Blower replied that he had not, but Dr. Patterson. had said she might use his name.—The Chairmen; Who. wrote the letter ?—Mrs. Blower: I had It written for ma—The ' Clerk : You should have told the magistrates that when , you handed it in.—The Chairman : The intentio; was just to convey the information that tbe doctor gave.—The case was then adjourned until the next court day. Nathaniel Johnson, of Earlestown, as summoned for a similar offence, and the defendant pleded guilty. lie said Mr. Cooper, the vaccination officer, had never asked him to have his child vaccinated, although he hadthe care of the child.—Mr. Cooper: I have been to your house and asked your wife.—The defendant : That is not me.—Mr. Cooper My duty is to visit the house and make inqpiries. I ask the mother if the father is not in.—The Chairman: What order do you ask for ?,—Mr. Cooper: For an'order for vaccination, within 21 days.—The Clerk (to defendant): Have you shy- ' thing to say why the child ohould nett be vaccinated?— There was no answer, and the Chairman asked: Do you I intend to have the child vaccinated ---Defendant No, sir, I do not.—The Chairman : We make an order that the child be vaccinated within 21 days, and the costs._ ... • .._

„ James Farr, of Earlestown,_was summoned for failing to have his child vaccinated. He said be pleaded guilty, hat he thought every father ought .to have the custody of his child and to say whether he had it vaccinated or not.. He bad strong objections to its bang vaccinated.—ln reply to the Chairman Mr. Coonf.r said there was nothing special in that case—The defendant said there should not be an order made upon him for BeVerdi reasons. He had two sisters and they were,bad altar vaccination. One sister's arm zei t breaking out with disease for many mouths after being vac.

oinated by the late Dr. Noon, and both sisters died as if they had wasted away. He had a sister livinz now who had been vaccinated twice, and two months after being vaccinated the second time she was seized with smallpox. He thought a father had a right to look after his own child, and be hail strong objections to his child being vaccinated. The de- ' fendaut then raised his child in the box and remarked I don,t think she wamts vaccination. Look at her ; I don't think i will make her any better. (A. laugh.)--The Chair- man : The Bench have carefully listened to what you have said. It is hardly necessary for me to tell you in reply , what the law is. There is no option left to.us here—we are I here to administer the law as it is. We are sorry to 11,ar of the cases to which you allude, but we have no alternative, and we grant an order for the caild to be vaccinated within

21 days.--The defendant: Would your. -worship; die-in-is; the costs of this ease, because I know there will he costs enough after.—Mr. Cooper : I ask for the costs, your wor- ships.—The Chairman : If we take the costs off in year case we should not be acting fairly to others, and we cannot do it—The defendant: I think I have geod grounds for asking it.—The Chairman : If we bad any optioe in the matter we might consider it, but we have no option.—The defendant : I would sooner take she smallpox to-morrow than have her vaccinated.

Joseph Jones, of Earlestown, was summoned for failing to take his child after being vaccinated to be inspected and examined by the vaccinator to ascertain the result of the j operation.—The defendant said he was guilty through ig- norance. He did not know that be had to take his child to the doctor after it had been vaccinated.—Mr. Cooper said the defendant was not saying what was true. He had given due notice to the defendant's wife that tne child must be inspected.—ln reply to. the Bench, the defendant expressed I his wilingness to comply with the law, and the case was dismissed on payment of costs.

div.head: COLONEL McCORQUOD ALE ON EDUCATION. _ _ _
div.p: COLONEL McCORQUOD ALE ON EDUCATION. _ _ _

On Saturday afternopn Colonel McCorquodale, the Liberal candidate for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, laid the foundation stone of a new school- chapel, in connection with the Independent Methodists, at Bryn, near Aehton. There was a large attendance. Mr. Worthington was called upon to present a silver trowel and ebony mallet to Colonel McCorquodale with which to lay the stoue. He had great pleasure in asking Colonel McCor- quodale to lay the stone, because, although that gentieman did not belong to the same church as themselves, yet they knew they had the colonel's hearty sympathy in thew efforts to train their children. In any undertaking which had that object for its aim, he knew no man who would be mere ready to assist than Colonel McCorquodale. (Loud ap- plause.).—Colonel. McCorquodale, who was warmly re- ceived, said, in the course of his address: As Mr. Worthing- ton observed, we are not all members of the same Church, but we have the same one great aim. lain not sufficiently acquainted with the Nonconformist customs to enable me to allude pointedly to the work you have undertaken so far as your chapel is coecerned, but I am satisfied as to the sincerity of your belief and the good work you take in hand when you assemble together. We of the Church should welcome all who take the Bible for their guide, and endeavour to worship in sincerity and tipth. If there be any difficulty in alluding to places of worship, where those who are assembled belong to various denominations, there should not be any delicacy regarding education. That is the most importent and engrossing subject of the present day, and we can all meet on common ground. Previous to 18e70 it was not compulsory for parents to educate their children in this country, and as a consequence many per- sons remained uneducated—some, indeed, could nether read eor write their own names. As a general rule, this lack of education prevented the people from making progress ; but there are some instances where it has not prevented persons from being successful in life. Colonel McCorquodale proceeded to point out the benefits of cheap newspapers, and the advantages conferred by the introduction of the penny post into the country. He went on to say that schools in that part of Lancashire were well managed, and religious education was carefully attended to. There could not be a question as to the usefulnese of the Bible; many of its passages had become as household words—they guided them in times of difficulty and trouble; and it inculcated all that which was calculated to elevate the character as well as to alleviate the sufferings of frail , nature. In conclusion he said :—ln our own country at the present time the law provides that boards of guardians may pay the school fees in cases where parents ,are not able to do so. But there are a great many persons who are against adopting this coarse of appearing before the boaeds on account of it looking like going for relief. (Hear, hear.) They had an idea that something might be done to alter that, and in that opinion I agree with them. (Hear, hear.) Another course might be adopted, viz., giving school attend- ance committees power to inquire into cases requiring aesistance. The committees meet usually about once a month, and as school matters are brought before them, I think they could relieve parents from attending before the guardians, and doethe work quite as satisfactorily. I hope the law will be altered so that this matter can be arranged. (Hear, hear.) As to religion, I may say th tt I noticed ia the Times of the 3rd inst. that Cardinal Manning made use of the following words, "It was religion that made Eng- land one, for it was never one until it became Christian. It made England free with the only freedom that could exist among men; it made England self-governed, for it made Englishmen govern themselves." (Hear, hear.) I venture to say that if you and I apply ourselves prooerly to the work and take advice from the wise man—" train up a child in the way he should go "—we shall be well rewarded, for the promise is that "when he is old he will not depart from it." I can only say-that I wish you every success re- specting this new school-chapel which I trust will be a blessing to the neighbourhood. I wish you God-speed, and Ido it most heartily. (Loud applause.)—An announce- ment was made that Colonel McCerquodale had contribu- ted £lO towards the funds.—ln proposing a vote of thanks to Colonel McCorquodale, Mr. S. Woods said be did not know any man who was more willing to promote the well- being of his countrymen than Colonel McCorqeodale, to whom he was sure they were much indebted for his presence and excellent address.—The motion was seconded by Mr. Price (Wigan), and carried with acclamation. The trowel bore the following inscription :—"..Presented to Colonel McCorquodale, J.P., of Newton, on the occasion of his lay- log the foundation-stone of the Independent Methodist School Chapel, Brynn, June 27th, 1885." As Colonel Mc- Corquodale drove from tne ground he was heartily cheered —A public meeting was held in the evening, and addresses were delivered by the Rev. IL Wilson, Mr. Brimelow, Mr. Worthington, etc.—The day's proceedings were a great SUCCOSS.
