ANTI-VACCINATIONT.—A meeting of delegates from seven anti-vaccination societies in L incashire, including Earles- town, was held at Mr. Duxbury's Temperance Hotel, Black- burn, on t..aturday, to take into consideration the advisability of; forming the whole of societies mentioned into a union for propas:ancLet work, for the insurance agai net fines for non-vaccination, and to assist one another generally in offering the most strenuous opposition to the Vaccination Act. Mr. Duabury was voted to the chair, and Mr. Miller, of Wigan, was elected secretary. After some discussion, it was unanimously decided that the scheme be adopted and carried out forthwith. _ _ _

THE LATE NEWTON RACES : DRIVERS FlNED.—Be- fore Colonel George McCorcmodale, Messrs. It. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, several cases of obstruction of the highway during the recent Newton races were heard. Alfred Taylor was summosed for obstructing Railway-street, Earlestown, on the 11th ult., by allowing his waggonette to stand therein, lie was fined 2s 6d and costs.—Joseph Wil- kinson, for committing a similar offence in Mill-lane, Newton, on the 11th inst., was also fined 2s 61 and costs.— Charles Ramsden was summoned for obstructing Mill-lane, Newton, by allowing an omnibus, drawn by three horses, to stand therein. As there was a doubt in the case the Bench dismissed it. The defendant asked the Bench if he could I have the names and addresses of two constables whom he alleged had damaged his omnibus. 'The Bench said they I could be obtained from Superintendent Jackeen. ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, William Walmslev, of Earlestowe, was charged under a warrant with assaultmg his wife, Mar- garet Walmsley, on the 25th April.—Mr. Browne, of War- ringtoin, appeared for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty. I—The1—The complainant stated that on the date named her hus- band threatened to give her two black eyes, and he then struck her.—Mr. Browne: What is he in the habit of giving 1 you per week ?.—Complainant: What I can get. (A laugh.) —Mr. Browne urged that there was no case against the de- fendant, and explained that when the summons came on for hearing the husband had been sent by his employer to repair some machinery in Yorkshire. On his return he imme- diately gave himself up to the police;but arrangements had been made for him to appear there that morning, and he was liberated.—The Bench remarked thit it was a painful case, that they did not think there was sufficient evidence to warrant a conviction, and the charge would be dismissed. BOLTON CONSERVATIVES AT NEWTON. The annual pic-nic in connection with the &dim and District Conser- vative Workingmen's Association was held at Winwick and , Newton on Saturday afternoon. The special train, which conveyed some hundreds of excursionists, left Bolton shortly after half-past two and arrived at Newton Bridge about half an hour later. They were accompanied by a brass band who played selections of music along the road to Winwick where the majority of the visitors, who had ac- companied the band, visited the church "and ether attrac- tions," as stated in the handbill. On returning to Newton the lake was the chief attraction. Arrangements had been completed for the excursionists to have the boats at reduced rates, while others spent the evening in dancing to the strains of the band in a field behind tne Pied Bull Hotel. The weather was beautifully fine and the large influx of visitors gave Newton an animated appearance. The special train returned from Newton abeut nine o'clock.

- EAP.mtsiown GOOD TEMPLAR& —The weekly session of the Bope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Template on Monday evening was of an unusually enjoyable character. There was a large attendance of members. The evening's programme was "A Night with our Juveniles," and in ac- cordance therewith about twenty members of the Juvenile Temple were admitted An excellent programme of songs, recitationg, Etc., was effectively gone through, under the presidency of Bro. James Barnard, in the absence of the Worthy Saperintendent (Bro. E. Nawman>. At the closs of the entertainment the lodge resumed its session and transacted several items of business. "Mail-bag night" was the feature of the proceedings. Interesting communi- cations, bearing well wishes for the future success of the lodge, were read from Bro. Thomas ilumpherson, district chief Templar of the Warwickshire District Lodge •, Bro. W. J. Woollen, P.V.D , of Sheffield; Bro. W. G. Erring- ton, P.D.E.D., Cheltenham, East tiloocestershire ' • and from Bro. George Hutcheson, reporter, of Buckle, Banff- shire, the latter having formerly been employed as a re- porter in Earlestown. The Worthy Secretary of the lodge was instructed to send the thanks of the lodge to the friends who had sent communications, and fraternal greetings to the lodges with which they were connected. PRESENTATION TO AN ODDFELLOW.—The half-yearly meeting of the members of the Loral Viaduct Lodge of Oddfellows, MU., was held at the Wellington Inn, Earles-

town, on S;.turia.; week. There was a large attendance of members, and Brother James Seddon, N.G, presided. The feature of the evening's proceedings was the presentation of a splendidly illuminated address to P.G. Matthew Jolley, of Haydock, the oldest member of the lodge. The address acknowledged the appreciation of P.G. Jolley's valuable services rendered to that lodge and oddfellovrship in general.

It continued :—"lt is with. great pleasure inat-we te- cord here your long and honourable connection with this lodge, for a period extending over 43 years—a great portion of which time has been spent officially, as your title denotes that you hive held all the distinguished offices of the lodge with ability and kindness, which has not pas- sed without observation, and we have been greatly benefitted and instructed by your wise counsel and advice upon all matters of importance relating to the business of the lodge, which has won for you the confidence and esteem of those with whom you have been brought into contact. We are conscious of the many arduous and difficult duties that have devolved uprm you in your official career; when the suc- cess or failure of the lodge (to a very great extent) depended upon your devotion thereto—a circumstance both discouraging and irksome--but we are glad to testify that those onerous duties have been unostentatiously per.formed by you with the'greatest pleasure and efficiencyond it Is to your untiring enemy that the lodge has grown up to its present flourishing numerical and financial position, which we think is very gratifying to you, and a noble example for us, your younger brethren, to emulate. We feel that this is only a small recognition of your services to the lodge, vet we treasure the hope that as such it will be accepted by you, and that you will be able for many years to come to look back with pleasure and satisfaction upon the period of your long and intimate connection with this lodge.—Signed ou behalf of the members, JA.I4ES SEDYPON, N.G., HENRI WORSLEY. JoH.N ECSERSLEY, Sec., June 20th, 1885." P.P.G.M. Thomas Tunstall made the presentation on behalf of the lodge, and highly eulogised the services of P.O. Jolley who, be said, worked as no other man did, and if it had not been for his untiriag services the Viaduct Lodge would not have been what it was.—P.P.o-.M. John Walker also spoke in high terms of P.G. Jolley's servicas.— P.G. Matthew Jolley, whourras received with loud applause, acknowledged the gift in appropriate terms.—On the motion of D.P.G.M. Win. Gilmour, seconded by P.1'.131.111, Tunstall, a cordial woe of thanks was paid to the secretary (PG. John Eckersley), fug drawing up the address. A sigglar compliment was paid to the committee and the proded- tugs coucladed.

General Grant's doctors say that be is gradually sinking, .nd must soon pass away. His voice is again inaud- inle, and his condition is one of extreme weakness. The new Lord Lieutenant of Ireland (the Earl of Carnar- von ) and his Chief Secretary (Sir W. Hart Dyke) arrived at the Viceregal Lodge, Dublin, on Monday evening. THE CLIFTON HALL COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—The Coro-
ner's ir quiry as to the cause of the Clifton Hall Colliery .xplosiiin was continued at Pendlebury on Wednesday. A miner named Price said he had complained to the over-

ooker Doxey (who was killed in the explosion) as to the '3 tate of the roof of the wagon-ways. Doxey told him the b•st thing he could do was to " shut his mouth." He also oemplained to a fireman named Thomas Hall, and some ,harp words were the result. The manager, in the witness's opinion, was competent and strict in the discharge of his duty, but be was deceived by those under • him. Fbe inquest was again adjourned. The principal . .

- witness, on Thursday, at the adjourned inquiry was he manager, Mr. Jonathan Hall. He expressed the opinion that the explosion had been caused by a very largo quantity of gas, but he believed that gas to have been latent, and undiscoverable by any human being. With respect to the use of naked lights in the Trencherbone mine, he said he bad always held the opinion that the only light with which a pit could be worked safely was that of the wifely lamp. So long as he remained manager of the col- liery no more naked lights should be used. The inquiry was adjmrued until Wednesday next. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. In the political world the principal business of the week has been the re-election of Ministers. In the majority of cases these have not been opposed. Where opposition has been instituted it has been for reasons of a personal character. In Launceston, the electors had the right, which they vigorously exercised, of protesting against an arrangement by 'which they were used as a step ladder for an ambi- tious lawyer. There was something particularly awkward about all the arrangements connected with the advancement of Sir Hardinge Giffard— his return of his briefs, his clutching at them again when the famous "hitch" in the Ministerial ar- rangements presented itself—his obliging presenta- tion to Mr. Webster of his seat at Launceston—if he could get it; Mr. Webster's anxiety during the hitch, and his uncertainty whether after all there would be any vacancy in the borough. These inci- dents, completed by the long delay in naming the law officers of the Crown, consequent upon the un- certainty of the election at Launceston, combined to present the Ministerial neachinery in an exceed- ingly cranky condition. How well founded was the doubt is shown by the result of the poll, the majority of the Conservative candidate in an ancient Tory stronghold being reduced by considerably over one half. At Woodstock and Eye Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr. Asbrnead Bartlett have not been permitted to resume their seats without a contest. In both cases the Liberal cause has suffered by reason cff the absence of personal influence and standing on the part of the candidates. Both at Woodstock and Eye the gentlemen who volunteered as Liberal clampions are what is known in political parlance as carpet baggers. Mr. Hawkes, who fought Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, was not only a self-appointed champion, but he came forward in opposition to the wishes of the local Liberal leaders, who do not seem to have thought it worth while to fight in view of the very short period the election would cover. Mr. Corti° Grant, who conceived the admirable notion of acquiring notoriety by opposing the parliamen- tary cock on his own dunghill, was for some time on the reporting staff of a London newspaper.' Since losing his appointment, he has hung about on the skirts of journalism, and has gone to swell the army of briefless barristers, so largely recruited from the -ranks of the Parnellites. Even with these weapons a stout fight has been made, and full opportunity provided for discussing the particular style of par- liamentary manners, of which Lord Randolph Churchill and Ashmead Bartlett are examples. There is'very little of either curiosity or interest in the approach in meeting of Parliament under its new management. The country rests content with • the assurance that the new Ministers can do no harm, or hardly any. The effort made to induce lilr. Gladstone to bind himself hand and foot indi- cated a desire for mischief. Had that audacious plan succeedea, and had the Opposition entered upon the new state of things pledged not to oppose, all kinds of things might have happened. Mr. Chaplin might have succeeded in sending butcher's meat up to famine price by stopping the importation of foreign cattle; trade might have been thrown into'a state of disorder by the appoint- ment of a Royal Commission upon protection principles; and we Might have had a war with Russia. But the new Opposition will approach its work absolutely untrammelled, and is determined to stand no nonsense. Acknowledging, this state of things, it will be to Lord Salisbury's interest to get business wound up in the Commons as quickly and as quietly as possible, so as to obtain a few months untrammelled enjoyment of office previous to the day, of reckoning. One act of the new Government which will be immediately challenged is the appointment of Sir Henry Wolff to the office of British Commissioner in Egerpt. Nothing could more forcibly illustrate the hopelessness a Lord Salisbury's position than this. Lord Salisbury, it need hardly be said, is both shrewd and capable man. He is as well able as anyone else to estimate the character of Sir Henry Wolff and his suitability for the Commission to which he has been appointed. No one with a por- tion of his knowledge on the subject could imagine that he would, other things apart, select Sir Henry as the best possible man for the post. But there are • other things that cannot be kept apart. Sir Henry Wolff, following the lead of Lord Randolph . Churchill, has distinguished himself by the violence of his vituperation of the present Khedive. Murder, robbery, and arson are some of the minor crimes for which they have .publicly indicted the Khedive. And now Sir Henry Wolff is selected as the emissary ' of Great Britain to Cairo I This must have been a bitter pill; but, presented by the resolute hand of Lord Randolph Churchill, Lord Salisbury swallowed it. The HOMO of Commons will, however, have its say on the subject, and the majority will probably make their first indication of resolve to safeguard the honour and dignity of the country by passing a resolution condemning this monstrous appointment. What a pitiful story is .this being unfolded day by day before three learned and prosaic judges, with Earl Redesdale (looking more than ever like a but- ler belonging to a good family) in the chair. Every- body knows how, ten years ago, the present Duke of Marlborough seduced and finally .ran away with the wife of the Earl of Aylesford. Lord Aylesford and he were intimate friends who drank together, betted together, borrowed money from the same usurers, and lived in sweet companionship. To add further piquancy to the episode, Lord Bland- ford had a wife of his own, sister to Lord Gebrge Hamilton, with whom Lord Randolph Churchill now sits in Cabinet Council. In 1875 Lord Ayles- ford went out to India with the merry party accom- panying the Prince of Wale, and the ' opportunity was deemed suitable by his familiar friend to sneak into his house through back doors and steal away his wife. This much was matter of common in- formation, for in various ways the case has occu- pied the courts of law. Now for the first time the veil is lifted from the misery of the woman whom Lord Blandford toyed with, and after a year or two, deserted. Nothing could 'be more pathetic than the first letter Lady , Aylesford wrote to the Dowager Countess announc- ing her flight. "You do not know," she writes, and you never can know how hard I have tried to win his (Lord Aylesford's) love without success, and I cannot live unc,ared for." Of this model hus- band's nearest friend the unhappy lady writes in another letter: " My God ! If it had been possible for me to give him up I would have done; but I cannot tell you how awfully I love him. It is the only excuse lam able to give you. The neglected wife, the deserted paramour, victim of two men who if they were not Peers of the Realm and here- ditary legislators might be called consummate scoundrels, has been living in retirement for several years and now comes forward in the effort, evi- dently hopeless, of securing the title for her son, born long after she had fled in despair and disgrace from Packington Hall. I hear from a personal friend of Miss Florence Warden that "The House on the Marsh," the suc- cessful novel not very successfully dramatised, is practically a narration of personal experience. Some ten or twelve years ago Miss Warden went as governess to a house where all the mysterious per- formances carried on at the "House on the Marsh" Were of actual occurrence. After this early and somewhat startling experience in life, Miss Warden, with her sister, went on the stage. They accom- panied Mrs. Langtry on her first visit to America; but fame did not dawn upon Miss Florence Warden till she cunningly built up the "House on the Marsh." The disposal of honours his, naturally enough, *ailedi up many inquiries. One persistently put s why Mr. Henry Edwards was knighted? As far as is known to his many friends, the new knight has only one claim upon the attention of the world. Ile gives almost the best dinners in London. Dinner Frying is, with him, both a science and an art. It 29 said he lies awake at night thinking over the arrangement of a menu. HypercriticscomPlain that he is a little exigeant in demanding recognition of the good things on the table, introdumng every course with a eulogy, and elaborating a biography for every bottle of wine. Still his dinners are un- commonly good, and are not likely to be worse now he is knighted. The puzzle remains why he should receive this special honour. Mr. Gladstone has a good healthy appetite, but he is not a gourmet, and • vsould not appreciate Mr. Edwards' dinners even if he partook of them, and I never heard that he did. Possibly Sir Henry got his knighthood as Lord Bra- bourne got his peerage—by asking for it. His hankering after a title is a standing jest among his friends. They have, indeed, long ago found him with a title. "Lord Linseed" he is called, with delicate reference to the particular article of pro- duce judicious dealing in ,which enables him in later days to dispense profuse and well directed hos- pitality. Among artists Mr. Watts, who has declined a baronetcy, is much more popular than Mr. Millais, who accepted it. The question with them is what will Sir Frederick Leighton think, and the general opinion is that the Preeid4nt will not be over

pleased. He is only a knight, whilst Millais is a baronet, and will, outside the walls of the Royal Academy, take precedence of him. Millais, who is widely popular, has received many congratulations , upon his new estate. One of his old acquaintances I asked him at a friendly supper the other night what Ihe was to call him now. "Call me Jack, as you always do," said the new baronet. "But for heaven's sake never omit to address my wife as 'your ladyship.'" I hear of a very singular concert that is to be given shortly. lam not sure whether the public will have admission, but the first performance will be before Her Majesty. It seems that the Belgian Government has an almost unique collection of old musical instruments. Their value is their rarity and their antiquity. There is a flute with but one key, a specimen of fabulous date, fifteenth century at the very latest; and a kind of clarionet which it needs an expert to get sound out of. The pro- gramme is to consist of music as far as possible , contemporary with the instruments. Mr. Irving has, accidentally I fancy, created a novelty in dramatic management. I remember four or five years ago at Portesma, when the Bancrofts and Arthur Cecil first visitedithe place, they gave a little performance for the benefit of a charity. The play selected was "The Vicarage," chiefly because it , was a three-part piece, and the result was that there was an enormous gathering of parsons. From all the neighbouring places English chaplains of all forms of ritual hurried up, and heard (without sin, for it was at an hotel, and not in a theatre) a beau- tiful moral play perfectly interpreted. Mr. Irving cannot, indeed, describe the Lyceum as an hotel. The glare of the footlights is over it all. But the Bishops have come forward handsomely (in their aprons) and patronised "Olivia." Shovel hats are stowed under stall seats, and, to an extent that tells admirably for the discipline of the church, curates and rectors follow the lead of the overseer of their \dioceses and bring every night to the theatre fresh feeling and hearty admiration. This is all very well; but when, next November, Mr. Irving takes the part of " Mephisto," •in t‘ Faust," what will the, sympa- thising Bishops say or do? Mr. 'Edward Clarke has been sadly disappointed that he is not orie of the law officers. Mr. Webster's selection has been a surprise. He is an extremely I sound lawyer. Had he been raised to the Appeal Court the bench would have been strengthened; but he is no advocate and a poor speaker. He has necessarily had no experience in politics, and can be of little use in the House. One explanation I heard was that his appointment was due to Lord Selborne's influence; they are personal friends and of the same school of religious conviction. The Prime Minister and the late Chancellor are, everyone knows, connected by the marriage of their children. ,

LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN. ADDRESSES BY MR. BRUNNER. A meeting Of the electors of the East Ward of the town. comprising Irwell-lane. Heath.road, Halton-road, Canal- street and the connecting streets, was held in Bethesda School-room on Tuesday night. There was a very good attendance, and Mr. J. R. Frith, chairman of the ward, oc- cupied the chair. On the platform were Mr. J. T. Brunner, Liberal candidate for the .Northwich Division. Messrs. J. N. Lello, W. Jepson, S. Fops, and W. Handley. The Chairman, in a vigorous speech, referred tO the pleasure it afferded him to be able to address almost all in that room as "fellow electors "—(bear, bear)—and allud- ing to the history et the Liberal party for toe past 50 years, said the progress made in Liberal politics during the past few years had been something extraordinary, and the ' party had to congratulate themselves upon the position they , held. They could not forget such men as Cobden and Bright—(applause)-110111 who had fought against great odds to obtaira for their fellow-countrymen those privileges which were their birthright, and now through the instru- mentality of the greatest statesman that ever lived—(ap- platts)—every householder in the town and country had the franchise. (Loud applause.) They were met that evening not to meet a stranger but to meet a friend. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They were there to meet Mr. Brun- ner and hear his views, and also to help each other in the great work of aAvancing the Liberal cause. There had been very little dens. In Runcorn in party poli- tico except at election times when a fight was coming on, but this system of waiting until the battle had been swept , away and they were now preparing for the fray. (Hear, heir.) Every elector was expected to aid. In former days othsr people had taught for them, and it was now their pri- vilege and their honour to fight also. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party were now on the Opposition benches of the House of Commons—(laughter)-but they hoped and trusted that in a few writhe hence the majority would be on the other side of the House, and the man who had given his energies, his power, and his life for his Queen and country would be reinstated in the position which should enable him to pass anise measures which were needed, not only for this country, hut for Ireland (Loud applause). It was for those present and himself to work for this end. Applause). Mr. Brunner, who was received with lowa applause on rising, said he heard last week that the division of the town invited to meet there that evening was that which was , mainly inhabited by their friends from over the Channel, and he accordingly made up his mind to talk &aunt what he canceived to be our policy for the future with regard to thel government of Ireland and her connection with us. Let him first thank his friend Mr. Frith for the too flittering Terms in which he had spoken of him and say how very glad he was that there came from him no uncertain sound as to his Liberal principles. (Applause.) Mr Frith was said to be a man entirely in the right place as chairman of one of their divisions. After referring to the Reform Bill of 1832, Mr. Brunner went on to speak of Ireland. It would, be argued, be a great shame on their part and on his pert to neglect to deal with the present necessities of Ireland. They ought to carefully inquire into her many grievances, gener- ously to meet her just demands, consider with all care her national susceptibilities, and finally, he hoped, with God's aid to win her love. (Applitise.) The reforms that they had won in the teeth of tee aristocratic party of England they demanded for Ireland. (Hear, hear.) 1832 first put power into the hands of the middle classes in England. Tee reforms that had been won by the middle class from 1832 to au hid never betel exteeded to Ireland, bet he looked to them (the electors) to enable the Liberal party to win these reforms for Ireland,—(hear, heer)—and he meant to talk principally about one—the reform in Local Government. Now, reform in Local Government was won for England in 18399, but no share was extended to our brethren across the Channel. But one very great reform bad been won for Irel end atilt had not been gained for England, and that wee reform of the Land Laws. (Applause.) That one rerorm was dearly purchaseA, was hardly won in Ireland at a cost of bloodshed, and at a cern of such bitter suffering, was one which in principle they demanded for England, for Scotland, and for %Vales. (Applause.) lie was pleased to see that the Commissioners under the Land Act were still busy in their beneficent work. The last return they had laid before the Houses of Parliament was for the mouth of March in this year. He found that the Commissioners had Investigated in their court the rents of an area of land amounting in the whole to 22,606 acres. The rents amounted to £14,809, or 13s per acre, but the Commis- sioners had reduced that amount to £12,052, or IN 61 per acre. (Applause.) Would they consider for a moment what that meant. It meant that probably more than a thousand families, because the average holding was not as much as 22 acres, had been taxsd for the benefit of land- lords usually absentee, some 20 per cent., or 4s in the £ more than was jrvtly due. This was only one month; the Commissioners had been at work for four years, and slowly they had lifted from the shoulders of the suffering farming class a very heavy load of most unjust taxation. That was the work of one of Mr. Gladstone's Land Bills. (Ap- plause.) He demanded a reform like this for the three countries, and he should like to say one word in passing about the demands made by and on behalf of the Crofters in the north of Scotland. (Applause). He asked for their sympathies and their practical help by their votes for these men, who were suffering just as cruelly as any tenantry in Ireland had suffered. (Applause.) A. bill for the relief of the Crofters wee brought in by the late Home Secretary, Sir Wm. They wanted a Municipal -Reform Act for Ireland. (Applause.) Lie described the evils that arose through the present antiquated system, and he asked them to help him to amend this matter. (Ap.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE,

The annual meeting was held in the Commissioners' B eard.rootn, on Wednesday afternoon. Present: Dr. Steele (in the chair), Mr. John Simpson, Mr. W. Handley, Mr. F. A. Lake, and Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian).—The Librarian reported that during June there were 834 books issued from the lending department, an increase of 64 on the correspond- ir.g month last year; eleven volumes had been issued from the reference department., increase 6ve ; total issues, 845. The sale of catalogues, fines, eic., realised 93 101. A number of books and pamphlets had been presented to the Library. Accounts amounting to £l4 us Id were passed for payment. A letter was read from Mr. Meadowcroft, who suegested that the Liverpool evening newspapers would be a boon to frequenters of the reading-room—Mr. Handley rebutted an accusation tbet the committee had been using the ratepayere' money for political literature in favour of one party. 'They purchased the Daily News and Standard, and Daily Post and Courier; all the other literature was presented ; so that the committee had not spent the rate- payers' money for party literature. It would be unwise to do so.—Mr. Lake said the committee had avoided as far as possible the introduction of sectarian or political literature. Of course if individuals inundated the committee with pamphlets they could not refuse them, although they might deprecate their introduction.—lt was decided to place the Echo and Express upon the reading-room table.—Mr. Geo. Faraday Smith, of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, wrote with reference to the "Model of Runcorn" mentioned in these columns some time ago. He said the model em- braced merely the dock frontage from the Duke's House to the Caetle Rock. He would inquire whether the trustees wished to part with it. —The Libra, ian read his annual report. It was, he stated, gratifying to report tied the Free Public Library continues to bold ite place as one of the most popular and useful in- stitutions in the town. During the past year the library had been open 151 days, and 15,618 issues had been made, being a daily average of 103. The number of borrowers to whom tickets had been issued during the year was 608; of theee 416 were males, and 192 females. During the year 625 volumes had been added to the library, 306 of which had been purchased and 319 presented. The total number of volumes on the shelves is 3,116 ; 774 being woyke of reference. The reading-room which is open daily continues to attract an increasing number of readers, and is supplied with four daily newspapers, twenty weekly papers and periodicals, and 24 monthly magazines and reviews. To the abundance and variety of the periodical literature pro- vided in the reading-room must be attributed the decrease in the number of works of reference consulted, the number of volumes issued being 311 as compared with 549 last year. The number of volumes in the library had been consider- ably augmented by means of generous gilt', and the com- mittee in expressly:lg their thanks for the same would make special mention of those given by the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty's Treasury, Trustees of the British Museum, . .

MR. BRUNNER ON EDUCATION.—NtEETING AT RUNCORN LAST NICI EIT. Last night a meeting of the electors of the mid district of Runcorn was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, and Mr. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal candidate, was present to deliver an address. Mr. G. Bellamy presided, and on the platform were the Revs. W. Gaily (Northwicb), W. Valldet Mews:. J. R. Frith, W. Handley. and 0. Leak. The Chairman, is opening the proceedings referred to the extension of the franchise, and the important questions for future leeislation—Disestablishment of the State Church and the temperance qnestion. It did not in his opinion matter whether any man was sent to the House of Commons pledged upon these subjects, because they would be dealt with when public opinion demanded it. (Applause.) Ile then introduced the candidate Mr. Brunner, who was well received, spoke upon the sub- ject of education. He might tell them that 200 years ago there were in England only about 500 schools. By the year 1750 two thousand or thereabout charitable foundations had been established for the purpoee of primary education. It was a curious thing daring this time, when there was the greatest activity in the founding of charitable institutions, it was a very common sight outside drink shops to see a painted board bearing the inscription • " Here a poor fellew can get drunk for a peony; dead drunk for 21 and can have straight clean straw to lie on for nothing." (Laughter.) Cii, the good old times! (Loud laughter.) He asked them to compare this state of things with the results of the Education Act of 1870. There were now 16 millions of population living under school boards—(ap- plause)—and 10 millions living under school attendance committees. The Education At was characterised by the Clerical party as the "Godless Act." He described the ad- mirable results of the Act in the improvement of children; and he called them by a very different name to Godless. Mr. Brunner described the free scoot system of America, of which he spoke favourably, but said they had made the unit of schisol-mantgement too small, with the result that money had been short and the schools had been too small for an efficient staff. and the net result bad been somewhat of a faiiure. It had gone so far that in the State of Pennsylv mia'a school was kept open for the benefit of one family, and in the State of Massachusetts there was a time when a school was kept up for the benefit of one scholar. (Laughter). In the immediate neighhour- hood there were three School Boards, Aston, Ware- ham, and Daresbury, each of which had joined together several townships, and the circumstances he bad narrated of America were thus avoided. He considered the system of school fees most inefficient and most cruel. Ho had been a member of a school attendance committee, and he could assure them his heart had bled I when he hart been obliged to send befoie the magistrates la widow woman because she had not sent the eldest girl te I school who was wanted to mind the baby. (Hear, hear) In conclusion be warned them that a fieht WAS cumin.. between the aristocratic principles and democratic principles. (Ap- plause.) The Liberals were for the Democracy (applause)—and looked for the support of demos—of the people. He had to ask them to take their stand upcn the principle of government by the people and for the people—(hear. hear, and applause)—and when in after years they looked back upon this beginning of the new era they might boast that in that day they did their duty, and in that noble work had their share. tAp- plause.) The Rev. W. Vanse moved the following resolution : "That this meeting is of opinion that J. T. Brunner, Esq., is a suitable gentleman to represent this constituency in Par- liament, and pledges itself to use all lawfal means to secure his return at the next general election." (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Marsh seconded thr:motion. The Rev. W. Gaily supported the resolution in a stirring ing speech, during which he was frequently and loudly ap- plauded. The resolution was carried with enthus'astn. In replying, Mr. Brunner said the representation of labour had been spoken of. His idea of the duty of a member of Parliament was that he ought to treat every man in the division that he represented as equal—(ap- plause)—that the capitalist should not weigh in the balance as much as all the men he employed, and that the capi- talist should only count as a man, and just as a man who held the tools in his hand from morning until night. (Ap- plause.) A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meeting separated.

, and Mr. John Simpson.—The financial statement showed that the receipts were £228 88 id, including £173 Is 2d from the library rate, a balance of £3O 16s 31 from the pre- vious year and 7d placed in the contribution box in the reading-room. After paying all expenses there was a bal- ance in hand of £2B 61 10d. The sum of £53 11, 8d had been paid in salaries, £36 6s 10i for new books. £is 5s 7,1 for magazines and newspapers, £l6 is for bookbinding, and £3l Is for printing and stationery.—Mr. Handley moved that the report be adopted and printed.—Mr. Lake seconded. —Carried. RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held on Thursday at the Town Hall, Waterloe-road. Mr. T. Norman presided, and there were present Messrs. Dobeen, Williams, epeakman, Grice, Timmins, Lighthurn, Linaker (law clerk), Marshall (eecre- rotary), and Barker (surveyor). HEALTH OF THE TOwat. The monthly report of the Medical Officer stated that the number of deaths reeistered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 28 Of these.deatha 4 were c (used by convulsions, by meningitis, phthisis, 3 to natural decay and 1114FASMII9, 2to pneumonia, and diarrhoea, rheumatic fever, paralysis. premature birth, heart disease, asct.tes, strima, and spinal effusion accounted for one each, makimg a death rate of 221 per 1 000 per annum of the population. One inquest was held; total deaths 29. Of the above deaths 15 occurred amongst children 9 years and under, and of these 9 were under one year.—Mr. Dobson said the report was very satis- factory as showing that the town was free from epidemics. The deaths enumerated might have occurred at any season of the year. Mr. Speakman said he understood that Dr. Mouritz was unwell and incapacitated from attending to his duties. He wished to knew what course wonld ha adopted en that the health of Ow town should not suffer.—Mr. Dotson said the Medical Officer had a qualified assistant who would he able to perform the duties until the doctor's recevery.—The Chairman : Dr. McDougall is do- ing all be possibly can to assist him.—The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee contained a report of the Surveyor that complaints had been received as to the in- convenience can el by shopkeepers placing goods on the footpaths; also that the Runcorn Gas Company had not submitted plans for the gasometer, akc., in course of erection. Tne Surveyor was instructed to bee the Inspector of Police with reference to the placing of goods on footpaths by shop- keepers. The secretary was instructed to write to the Run- corn Gas Company, intimating that it will be necessary for them to submit plans of their proposed extensions. It was recommended that Mr. Meadowcroft be appointed a member f the Health (sub) Committee. The Health (cub) Committee had instructed the Secretary to write to Mr. Field. drawing his attention once more to the large number of ashpits requiring to be emptied, and informing him that the number oust be reduced without farther de- lay, or rigorous measures would be taken. It was recom- mended that the plan of William Farrell for the erection of I eight cottages at Mouth Bank be approved, subject to pro- viding ventilation for the hack bedrooms. Instructions to Secretary to write to the Archit-ct of the proposed Salva- tion Army Barracks, aeleing him to set the building further back so as to be in a line with the adjoining premises.— Mr. Speakman moved, awl Mr. Williams seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. 'Speakman wished to know whether or not the Health Committee had charge of the nightsnil contract. He understood the contractor was very much behind in his work, and having regard to the epidemic on the continent of Europe, it was necessary, as Runcorn was a port, that this work should be done promptly —The Chairman Baia the matter was in the bench of the Health Committee who wore doing all they posaibly could.—Mr. Barker said Mr. Fiold was 95 ashpits b:atind.—Mr. Dobson said he had been round the teem to ascertain its general sanitary condition. Ha was pleased to saw it had improved very much during the last two month% The Sanitary inspec- tor was exercising very good influence upon the tenants of the houses. He was going round frequently and impressing upon the people the necassity of having their houses clean in consequence of what may be expected from the conti- nent. Referring to the nightsoil contract. Mr. Dobson said when Mr. Field underto tk the work there were 140 or 150 ashpits wanted emptying, and lvt had not been as energetic as he might have been, but he had done exceedingly well. Last week, A boat he had carrying nlghtsoil sank in the canal and became a wrrck, and he had also lost a horse, so that .he had been unable to attend to the work as well as he might have done If be did not take steps to reduce the number

Queen's Bench is postponed for a week. Swine fever has broken out in two places at Luton, and is raging virulently in Bedfordshire.. On Thursday night some 9f Osman Digna's followers penetrated the Suakim lines and entered the town. Tim Queen visited the Duchess of Cambridge last even- ing. remaining about three-quarters of an hourrand returned to Windsor shortly before 7 o'clock. The steamer East Anglia spoke the Gal:ia on the 28th tilt, and took the mails. The Gallia afterwards fell in with River Avon. and was taken in tow by the latter. According to present arrangements, the Queen and Prin- cess Beatrice will leave Windsor for Osborne on the 16th inst., and remain there until after the Princess's marriage. At Dublin, on Friday, the Lord Chancellor called within the Bar Mr. Holmes, M.P., as Attorney-General, and Mr. Monroe, Q C., as Solicitor-General for Ireland. There was considerable applause in court. STIOCKING ACCIDENT.—At Bray Seawall Works, on Fri- day, a labourer named Joseph Kinsella was killed in- stantaneously, one of the iron buckets, which broke from the lifting chain, having fallen upon him and crushed him to death. A convention of Nationalists from all parts of County Down, numbering over 100 delegates, was held in Down on Friday, when a resolution was unanimously passed to actively support the Liberal candidate at the approaching contest. THE EVOLUTIONARY SQUADRON.—Ifer Majesty's torpedo ship Ilecla sailed on Thursday night from Bantry Bay, baying taken on board any remains of the mines left after the recent experiments. The squadron is timed to arrive to-morrow at Blacksod Bay. It may be detained by some special manoervres to be carried out en route. Ma. CnArairsamans has definitely fixed his visit to Hull for the sth and 6th August On the first day he will speak on general politics, and on the second be will address a meeting of seamen, aid in the evening attend a dinner at the United Liberal Club. From Hull he will proceed to Ireland, and subsequently be will visit Scotland. tons. ATTEMPTED MPRDER THROUGH JEALOI79Y.—WM. Burt was charged at Yarmouth, on Friday, with attempting the nuarder of his wife, Harriet Burt, and a man named John Andrews, by outing their throats. It was stated that Burt, on returning from sea on Thursday, ascertained that his wife, from whom he bad been living apart, was at An. drewe' house. It is alleged he went there, and in a fit of jealousy committed the crime. Mrs. Burt is not expected to recover. The prisoner was remanded. MIIRDER OF A SWEETHEART. At the Northampton 1 Assizes on Friday, Thomas Brooks, formerly a guard on the London and North-Western Railway, was brought up for the wilful murder of his sweetheart, at Stoke Bruerne, in March last. Brooks first shot .he young woman, and then his father and the latter's housekeeper ; but the last two recoveerd from their injuries. Evidence was given of the prisoner's insanity. He was, therefore not put on his trial, but ordered to be detained during Her Majesty's plea.

Woongrocx ELECTION. —The polling at Woodstock com- menced in each of the six districts at eight o'clock on Fri- , day morning. la the principal agricultural parishes—Bla- den, Handborough, Stonesfield„ Combe, Tackley, and Wootton—many labourers took advantage of the breakfast hour to poll. lo the town of Woodstock, however, the at- tendance at the hooths was small. The Duke of Marl. borough, who, before leaving Blenheim, bad directed that his horses were not to decked with party/ colours, countermanded the order by telegraph 011 Thursday night, and on Friday the horses wore Conservative colours. The polling during the morn- ing progressed slowly, especially in Woodstock town. It was stated that Sir Henry Daehavotefe example of ab- stention would be largely folloireti by the,Liherale; whereas almost every Conservative would poll. Mr. Grant and Lidy Churchill visited the principal palling places. The Conservatives had an advantage in the Duke of Marl- borough's and ether carriages, numbering 40, against 14 on the Liberal side. As the day advanced the Conservatives grew more sanguine, the only question being the size of Lord Randolph's majority. Everything was quiet. In the evening the poll was declared 119 follows :—Lord Randolph Churchill (C), 532; Mr. Corti* Grant (L), 405; Conser- vative majority, 127.
THE SHIP CANAL HILL.-CLOSE OF THE PROMOTER& CASE.

The Select Committee of the House of Commons, pre- sided over by Mr. Forster, sat again on Friday and heard further engineering evidence in favour of the Manchester Ship canal—Mr. Vernon Harcourt, civil engineer, who gave evidence against the bill last year and the year before, said. the present scheme was free from the objection urged against those previously prepared. He did not believe that the works proposed would cause a permanent settlement of the low water channel abut the side of the canal and pre- vent its wandering over the eetuary.—ln reply to the chair- man. the witness said Mr. Lyster's plan was net so good as Mr. Williams'.—After clearing the room for a short time, the chairman said the Committee were strongly of opinion considering the session might be very brief, that the pro- moters must close their case that day. It might be that witnesses would have to be called to clear up points, but they did not require further evidence except as to pilotage. —Mr. Pernber asked if he should call a witness to sperk of the feeling in Manchester with regard to the scheme.—The Chairman : No, von need not trouble about that. We knew there is plenty of fee ing both in Manchester and Liver- ttool.—Mr. Littler: There was, hat not bow.—Mr. Pero- ber : That is not the fact —Mr. J. A. Rutherford, a pilot, having been examined, the case for the promoters closed. The Case for the Mersey Board will commence on Mon- day with the engineering evidence.

div.head: FAILVRE.OF A WIDNES TRADESMAN.
div.p: FAILVRE.OF A WIDNES TRADESMAN.

At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Cowl, on Thursday, before Mr. Registrar Cooper, George LPWIS Merkel, who had car- ried on business as a hosier, batter, and general dealer in Widnes and Padiham, appeared for his public examination. His liabilities were stated to be £2lO, and his assets £45, includiug £3O stock in trade, the alleged cause of failure beiog general depression in trade and losses on resa.e of stock. Mr. Swift appeared for the debtor, who stated, in reply to the Official Receiver, that he had failed ten years ago at Stockport, and paid his creditor. 3s ad in the £. He opened his first shop in Widnes in 1873, having no avail- able cash but about £l5 worth of stock, and at the begin- ning of last year he opened a second shop in Waterloo-road, and a third establishment in Padiham. He was making sufficient profit in the first shop to pay his way, but he had overstocked himself. He opened the additional shops to get rid of the goods in hand; but he had lows through his goods continually going out of fashioo. At Christmas, 1884, he had nearly £2OO of stock in his pos- session, but in April he employed a Mr. Robert Jones, an auctioneer, of Widnes, to bold sales by auction in the shops on Saturday and Monday evenings. These sales continued for two monthc—The Official Receiver: Then you must have got through a quantity of stock 7—The debtor (wko spoke with a strong foreign accent) : Yes. All the stock was disposed of in this way, and he admitted that in April last he instructed his solicitor Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, to inform his creditors that he was solvent, and if they would allow him time for payment, he would make them an offer ef £l2 per month. When asked the meaning of the word "solvent" he was unable to reply, and said that insolvent mean a man's inability to pay his accounts. The Registrar remarked that this showed the debtor to have more know- ledge of insolvency than of solvency. Ultimately the mat- ter was adjourned until the 23rd, in order that the debtor might ale an account allowing his purchases and sales of stock.
STRANGE DEATU OF A SAILOR AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday -Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest at the Bridgewater Arms Hoiel, on the body of Henry Evans, aged 20, who died on Monday morn- 1 ing, in a dwelliog-house in Percival-lane. It appeared that Evans was a sailor on board the schooner " Agnes and Helen." On the 18th June he Was skulling a boat in the Fenton Dock, standing on the seat, when his oar slipped and he fell into the water. A youth named Robinson rescued the deceased from the water after he had been immersed about three minutes. The deceased changed his clothes, and helped to take the vessel up to the entrance of the Wes- ton Canal, afterwards going to bed. He apparently was in his neatl health, but on the following Wednesday the de- ceased was so ill that Dr. McLennan WAS sent for. The doctor discovered the patient lying in the cabin in the fore- cantle suffering from acute pleurisy and bronchitis. He prescribed let him and ordered his immediate removal from the cabin, which was in a most unhealthy and unfit condi- tion for a sick man, to some place where he could be taken care of. The captain was not OR hoard and the mate re- fused to take the responsibility. On the Friday the cap- tain returned to the vessel, and made an unsuccessful at- tempt to get the deceased sent to the Workhouse or the Hospital, but on Saturday he made arrangements for his re- InovaL Dr McLennan, owing to the stormy rate of the weather, declined to permit his removal at that time, and be Was not taken to a lodging-house in Percival-lane until Sunday, On Monday the unfortunate man died.—Dr. McLennan gave It as his opinion that deceased had died from pleurisy, complicated with bronchitis, due in all pro- bability to his imtnersiAn in the water.—Tbe Coroner said the question for the jury to decide was whether the deceased had come to his death through any negligence on the part of the mate who had declined to take the responaibility of his removal. The jury might think he was net deserving of censure because he was not willing to pl-dge the cap- t tin's credit in his absence for any expenditure that mikht be ineurred.—After some consideration the jury returned a "ratline in accordance with the medical testimony.

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS BANK.

A special meeting of the trustees and managers of this bank was held on Tuesday, in the Bank Buildings. Mr. John Brundrit. J.P., was voted to the chair, and there were present---the Revs. Canon Barclay, W. Preston, and E. Willienie; Messrs. Jaines Handley. J.P., Jnbra Simpson, W. whittiker. P. Speakman, J. 0. Jackson. W. Brooks, T. Handley, H. Forrester, S. C. Beckett, and W. F. Salkeld. The business of the meeting was to decide upon the future of the hank and the appointment of an actusry and trea- surer. The minutes of the committee deputed to deal with these suhinets were re-ad. The advisability 01. bringing the operltiens of the hank to a conclusion, and transferring, the accounts to the Post Office was under discussion. The cornmittee came to the unanirmaas opinion that the bank was a public convenience end benefit, and ought to be con- tinued. The actuary's salary was then fixed at .850 a year, An advertisement in the local papers resulted in applica- tions being received from Mr. Walter Jones, of South Bank Hotel, Mr. Arthur Crosby, Leinster Gardens, and Mr. Wm.

Handley, Bridge-street. On the motion of Mr. Simpson, I seconded by Mr. S. C. Beckett, the committee resolved that the name of Mr. Handley be recommended to the general I meeting of trustees and managers.—Mr. Simpson moved the adoption of the committee'. recommendations. The bank, he said, had done very well for many years past. Mr. Salkeld, the managers believed, had been the one great cause, if not the principal cause, of the success of the I bank owing, to his well-known character, his standing in the town, and his mature age, and the committee thought it would not be at all desirable to appoint too young a man to the position of actuary. So far as he knew the charac- ter of all the applicamts was all that could be wished for, and their sureties would be everything the bank would re- quire, but on the grounds he had named the committee thought Mr. Handley the most eligible applicant. Mr. Simpson highly eulogised Mr. Handley's character sad abilities as a financier, as shown by his career in public positions, and said he really did not think they could appoint a better man to succeed Mr. Salkeld. Mr. Beckett seconded the motion, and after explaining that there had been no collusion between himself and Mr. Simp- son, spoke in warm terms of praise of Mr. Handley,—The Rev. W. Preston, M.A., moved as an amendment the ap- pointment of Mr. W. Jones,who, he said, Mr. Salkeld had informed him on many occasions before this appointment was vacant, was fully competent to carry on the business, and he hal done so in a very eatisfactory manner during Mr. Salkeld's illnese--.The amendment, was not seconded, and the original motion was subsequently carried unani- mously.—Mr. W. Whittaker and Mr. J. 0. Jackson were each proposed for the office of treasurer, but declined, and eventually, amid the hearty applause of those present, Mr. Simpson consented to continue in office until the annual meeting in January.—On the motion of the Rev. W. Pres- ton, seconded by the Rev. E. Williams, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Simpson for his services and his present kindness.—On the proposition of Mr. James Han ley, seconded by Mr. P. Speakman, the Chairman WAS thanked for the manner in which he had conducted the proceedings —ln replying, Mr. Brundrit expressed his plea- sure that the bank was not to be given over to the Post- office, but to coatinue, he hoped, to flourish and be a benefit to the town.

div.head: ilitor.
div.p: ilitor.
AN n VACCINATION.

_ Sir—lt may be of interest to come of your readers just noir to learn that by the Vaccination Act, 1871, 34 and 35th Vict., chap., 98, sec. 11th, seven of the orders to vaccinate made on parents by the magistrates at Newton.le-Willows on the 31st of May last year have lapsed because not en- forced within twelve months from the date of the said orders being made. The Wigan appeal case, known as Knight v. Halliwell, clearly confirms this view, as well as the case deoided by the Court of Queen's Bench,. Miller v- RhinO, which distinctly sets forth that all orders, itc., under the Vaccination Acts must be proceeded with within twelve months, or new proceedings must be instituted.—Yours, 13.. HARRISON. Earlestown, June 30th, 1885.

div.head: WARRINGTON MAGISTIATES.
div.p: WARRINGTON MAGISTIATES.

Sir,—Attenders at Warrin.gt-on—Borough--dourt are be- ginning to learn by experience the truth of the old saying that "everybody's business is nobody's." Somebody remarked some time ago that there were as many magistrates in Warriogton as policemen. Since then some more have been created, and "J.P's." are about as plentiful as " Cap'ns " and " Kernels " in a backwoods town. It has been said that men could be divided into two classes, the rogues and the fools, but if this rate of magistrate-mak- ing is to be kept up in Warrington it will not be long before we will be able to divide, in a more complimentary way, the people of the town into the two classes of those who sit on the bench and those who stand in the dock. At all events one cannot go along the street without rubbing shoulders with one of the former class, and tbe place where they are beginning to bi most scarce is the police court at ten o'clock in the morning. It is to be hoped that the honour of administering justice is not the less prize d' in proportion to the number on whom it is bestowed. ' C. P.

div.head: "A SUBSTANTIAL CONSERVATIVE VICTORY."
div.p: "A SUBSTANTIAL CONSERVATIVE VICTORY."

Sir,—On Thursday eveiliW,Vhile-g-lan-cir;;;;;-Copy of an evening contemporary—the "neutral in all matters political and religious "—I came across a par,graph infor- ming its readers that " Two substantial Conservative vic- tories were recorded at the polling-booths yesterday." Well, I thought, if a professedly "neutral " journal goes out of its way to inform its readers that the Conservatives have gained" substantial" victories there must be something out of the common, or an unusually large majority. But on reading a little further I found that one of the so-called "substantial victories " referred to the election at Laun- ceston, where Mr. Robert Webster, the newly-apnointed Attorney-General, was returned by a majority of 43 votes over his Liberal opponent. If this can be termed a "sub- stantial Conservative victory," when it is remembered that at the previous election for the same borough, the Tory candidate had secured 105 votes more than his op- ponent, I am at a loss to understand what my Tory friends and their journals—although they may profess " neutrality "—will venture to describe the result of the next contest at the same rate of" progress "—so far as the- Liberals are concerned. I think Mr. Pdthick and his sup- porters deserve the thanks of every Liberal for the splen- did fight he made, by which the Tory majority of .1.05 was reduced to 43. There is every encouragement for the min- ority to hope for the future, and then, if the present elec- tion can be looked upon as a " substantial Conservative victory," another similar " victory " will result in a truly " substantial" defeat of the Tory candidate.—Yours, Jte., A WORKMAN.. I Warrington, 3rd July, 1885.

div.head: STOPPAGE OF THE FOOTPATH ACROSS THE
div.p: STOPPAGE OF THE FOOTPATH ACROSS THE
MESNES.

Sir,—On looking oveill-le-re-pn-rt of the last meeting of the Newton Commissioners which was reportei in your issue of 6th June, I rind it stated that the law clerk was in- strtacted to call upon Mr. Legh's agent to remove all ob- structions from the footpath between Crow-lane and the railway arch before the last dav of May. It is now the end of June and still the obstruction remains, or at least it did a few days ago when last I SAW it. Now the road laud has been unquestionably a public road ; in fact I should not be overstating the case if I said it was an historic one, and the Commissioners know it, and I say it will be to their everlasting discredit if they do not assert the rights of the public in this matter. .

_ I venture to sAy if I had done anything to incur the dis- pleasure of the Commissioners, and bring myself liable to an acticn at law as in this case, and had appeared to set them at defiance and treated them with contempt in the manner that Mr. Pardey has done throughout the whole of these proceedings, I say they would have dealt with me in a far more summary fashion than has been extended to him.

To our prospective member (and I am hoping he will be) I would say if he is desirous of showing that he is worthy of our suffrages and having our interests entrusted to his keep- ing, let him speak out plainly in defence of the rights of the public in his place in what I will call our local Parliament, and not exhibit the supineness that appears to prevail on _ . .

the Board on thie question. If the Commissioners fail in their duty, I hope the ratepayers will remember this when the election of Commissioners comes round, not forgetting Mr. Fairclough, who I think has acted very inconsistently with regard to this matter. Apologieing for troubling you so much, but hoping you may be able to find room for this—l remain, yours tru)y, A RATEPAYER,

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Betore Mr. W. Bankee and Caletain C. W. Hazieburst. DRUNICENNESS.—Jane Hicks and John Brannan were charged with being drunk in the Three Crowns beerhouse, Queen-street. and refusing to qeit when requested.—P.C. Wallace proved the case, and Hicks was fined lOs and costs. A warrant was issued for the apprehensioe of Brannan, who did not appear.:--Thos. Cline, contractor, was fined 51 and costs Se 101 for being drunk and incapable in High-street on Saturday night. P.C. Hamersley proved the case.--For being drunk on the 27th ult. W,n. Pritchard was fined 5s and costs 108 6 I. TIIESDLY.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Captain C. W. H tziehurst. REFCSING TO QUIT.—John Brennan was charged under a warrant with being drunk in the Three Crowns beeehouee and refusing to quit on the 23rd ult. He WAS tined 103 aid costs .183 41, or 21 days on the evidence of P.C. Wal- lace. DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and James Marson. DAMAGING PROPERTY.—Edward Savage, a lad, was charged with having damaged property belonging to Messrs Greenall. Whitley, and Co., at Stratton, on the 28th May Defendant was seen by a policeman to knock some bricks from a building near the public-house. Stratton, and it was stated that altuough this building, when bought by Messrs. Greenall three years ago, was intact there WAS now nothing but a gable end left, the rest having been destroved.—The defendant was ordered to pay lie 61, including damage and flee. STRAYING CATTLE.—For allowing cattle to stray On the highway at Little Leigh, on the 11th ult., George Young was fined 2s and costs. A NEGLECTED CGlLD.—George Hatton, a young lad, was charged with sleeping in an outbuilding, having no visible means of subsistence, on the 4th ult. It was stated that the lad was the son of a workman at Wilderspool Brewery, and the father being away all day he was altogether neglected. —Mr. da Prez. school atteedance officer, said that the lad had never been at school sinze his father was previously summoned.—The case was adjourned in order to allow the Attendance Committee to take action. SCHOOL ATIENDANCE.—James Wilkinson and Joseph Moss were each tined 5a for not sending their children regu- larly to school. ALLEGED OBSTRUCTION.—JOSeDh Smith was summoned for obstructing the highway at Stretton, on the 19th May, by putting a rail fence across the same, but as A question of right was raised the case WAS adjourned till after a meet in of the Highway Beard had been held.

GOLBORNE- SERMON ON THE CLIFTON HALL EXPLOSION.-011 Sun- day night the Rev. J. T. Carom, of aolborne, preaching at the Congregational Chapel. made special reference to the terrible explosion at the Clifton Hall Colliery, and gave some interesting incidents respecting the disaster. Mr. Camm made a special journey to the scene of the accident and in- terviewed officials and eye-witnesses, from whom he obtained much infomation respecting the victims and their families. A box was placed at the door in which donations were given at the close of the service on behalf of the relief fund. A letter has been received from Pendlebury by the Rev. J. T. Camm, acknowledging the receipt of the £3 18s Id which has been paid inM the bank. A WIFE'S MAINTENANCE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Monday, before Col. McCorquociale, Messrs. R. Houghton, J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, Thomas Broadhurst, a collier, residing at Golbrrne, was summoned, at the instance of Mr. A. Eccieston, relieving officer for the Leigh Union, to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the support of his wife, at present I confined in Rainhill Lunatic Asylum. Mr. Eccleston ex- plained that the defend mt's wife was removed to Rainhill asylum on the 30th February, 1884, and for a time the de- fendant paid 3s. per week towards her maintenance. He had, however, fallen into arrears amounting to £7 is. He was a collier in full work, and had no family.—The defen- dant said he had been out of work most of the time since his wife had been in the Asylum. He was willing te pay when could.—Thet Bench made an order for the payment of 3s. per week. STEALING CANNED MEAr.—Ann o.lllgan, a married woman from Golborne, was brought up at Mr. Backton's ffice, Warringten, on Monday, on a charge of stealing, on iaturday nieht. a tin of canned meat value Is. 4 I , from the I,hop of Mr. John Howe. High-street, Golborne. The case was adjourned until Wednesday. Prisoner was allowed out mbail. At the Warrington Coenty Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Ann O'Hagan was charged with hay- rig stolen from the shop of Mr. Hayes, High-strett, Gol- 'wire, a tin of tinned beef, value Is 4d, on Saturday night. It appeared that the prisoner had been making a trifling purchase in Mr. Hayes' shop, and was noticed to take the tin of beef. Information was given to the police, and on tier house being searched the beef was found there. She ..,:eaded guilty, and was fined 20s and costs, or in default, 14 days.
